papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we accelerate training of large transformer models by reducing activation recomputation, i.e., reducing memory consumption for activations without redundant compute?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation to reduce activation memory by 5x and recover over 90% of the compute overhead from activation recomputation.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents two straightforward techniques, sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation, which together reduce activation memory by 5x and recover over 90% of the compute overhead from activation recomputation.
papers.key_findings:
Sequence parallelism along with tensor parallelism reduces activation memory by distributing activations across the tensor parallel group.
Selective activation recomputation checkpoints only memory-intensive but computationally cheap parts of the transformer layer (e.g., attention operations), reducing recomputation overhead.
Combined, the techniques achieve a 5x reduction in activation memory and over 90% reduction in the compute overhead from activation recomputation.
For a 530B parameter model, the method achieves 29% faster training compared to using full activation recomputation.
The method achieves high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU), up to 56.3% for a 1T parameter model.
papers.limitation: Memory fragmentation for large microbatches and non-uniform memory allocation due to pipeline parallelism are not addressed.
future_direction: Further reduce activation memory by resolving issues from memory fragmentation for large microbatches and non-uniform memory allocation due to pipeline parallelism.
Work on methods to reduce memory pressure on the first stage of the pipeline.
papers.abstract: Training large transformer models is one of the most important computational challenges of modern AI. In this paper, we show how to significantly accelerate training of large transformer models by reducing activation recomputation. Activation recomputation is commonly used to work around memory capacity constraints. Rather than storing activations for backpropagation, they are traditionally recomputed, which saves memory but adds redundant compute. In this work, we show most of this redundant compute is unnecessary because we can reduce memory consumption sufficiently without it. We present two novel yet very simple techniques: sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation. In conjunction with tensor parallelism, these techniques almost eliminate the need to recompute activations. We evaluate our approach on language models up to one trillion parameters in scale and show that our method reduces activation memory by 5x, while reducing execution time overhead from activation recomputation by over 90%. For example, when training a 530B parameter GPT-3 style model on 2240 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, we achieve a Model Flops Utilization of 54.2%, which is 29% faster than the 42.1% we achieve using recomputation. Our implementation will be available in both Megatron-LM and NeMo-Megatron.

papers.title: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: How do minimal circuits for indirect object identification emerge in attention-only transformers trained from scratch on a symbolic task?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that task-constrained training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits for indirect object identification in attention-only transformers.
papers.conclusion: Task-constrained training can produce parsimonious and interpretable circuits, offering insight into computational motifs underlying reasoning in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer, two-head attention-only transformer achieves perfect accuracy on the symbolic IOI task.
The two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution.
A two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance through composition across layers via query-value interactions.
Positional embeddings improve accuracy and interpretability but are not strictly necessary for the task.
The circuits in task-constrained models are more parsimonious than those in broadly pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer large language models (LLMs) into human-understandable computational circuits. However, the complexity of pretrained models often obscures the minimal mechanisms required for specific reasoning tasks. In this work, we train small, attention-only transformers from scratch on a symbolic version of the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task -- a benchmark for studying coreference -- like reasoning in transformers. Surprisingly, a single-layer model with only two attention heads achieves perfect IOI accuracy, despite lacking MLPs and normalization layers. Through residual stream decomposition, spectral analysis, and embedding interventions, we find that the two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution. Furthermore, we show that a two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance by composing information across layers through query-value interactions. These results demonstrate that task-specific training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits, offering a controlled testbed for probing the computational foundations of transformer reasoning.

papers.title: Modularity in Transformers: Investigating Neuron Separability & Specialization
papers.research_question: How modular and task-specialized are neurons in transformer models? The paper investigates the overlap and specialization of neurons across different tasks and data subsets.
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence for task-specific neuron clusters in transformers, showing that neuron importance patterns are partially present even in randomly initialized models and are refined by training.
papers.conclusion: The methods reveal interpretable modularity in transformers, and the overlap between random and trained models provides evidence for a weak Lottery Ticket Hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific neuron clusters exist in transformers, with varying degrees of overlap between related tasks.
Neuron importance patterns persist to some extent even in randomly initialized models, suggesting an inherent structure that training refines.
MoEfication clusters correspond more strongly to task-specific neurons in earlier and later layers of the models.
For ViT, classes with intuitive similarities (e.g., 'insects' and 'non-insect invertebrates') show higher overlap in selected neurons.
For Mistral, unlearning a text subset (e.g., 'PubMed Central') leads to performance drops in related MMLU subjects (e.g., 'professional medicine').
papers.limitation:
We focused on MLP neurons and did not analyze attention mechanisms, which play a crucial role in transformer models.
Our analysis was limited to a specific set of tasks and datasets, and may not generalize to all domains or model architectures.
The interpretation of neuron importance and specialization is still somewhat qualitative and could benefit from more rigorous statistical analysis.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to include attention mechanisms and their interaction with MLP layers.
Developing more sophisticated clustering techniques that can capture hierarchical relationships between neurons and tasks.
Investigating how neuron specialization evolves during the training process.
papers.abstract: Transformer models are increasingly prevalent in various applications, yet our understanding of their internal workings remains limited. This paper investigates the modularity and task specialization of neurons within transformer architectures, focusing on both vision (ViT) and language (Mistral 7B) models. Using a combination of selective pruning and MoEfication clustering techniques, we analyze the overlap and specialization of neurons across different tasks and data subsets. Our findings reveal evidence of task-specific neuron clusters, with varying degrees of overlap between related tasks. We observe that neuron importance patterns persist to some extent even in randomly initialized models, suggesting an inherent structure that training refines. Additionally, we find that neuron clusters identified through MoEfication correspond more strongly to task-specific neurons in earlier and later layers of the models. This work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of transformer internals and offers insights into potential avenues for improving model interpretability and efficiency.

papers.title: Multi-head Transformers Provably Learn Symbolic Multi-step Reasoning via Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve symbolic multi-step reasoning problems via chain-of-thought processes, specifically path-finding in trees, through gradient descent training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that one-layer multi-head transformers can learn symbolic multi-step reasoning via chain-of-thought through gradient descent, with attention heads specializing and coordinating to solve path-finding tasks, and provides generalization guarantees to unseen trees.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that one-layer multi-head transformers can learn symbolic multi-step reasoning via chain-of-thought with provable optimization and generalization guarantees, offering mechanistic insights into how transformers implement algorithmic procedures.
papers.key_findings:
One-layer transformers can learn to solve backward and forward path-finding tasks in trees via chain-of-thought reasoning.
Multi-head attention heads autonomously specialize and coordinate to handle multi-stage reasoning, with one head performing path-finding and another controlling stage transitions.
Gradient descent training dynamics converge to parameters that implement the desired reasoning mechanisms.
The learned models generalize to unseen tree structures, learning generalizable rules rather than memorizing paths.
Extending reasoning length via chain-of-thought allows shallow transformers to solve complex tasks that might otherwise require deeper architectures.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multi-step reasoning tasks. However, understandings of the underlying mechanisms by which they acquire these abilities through training remain limited, particularly from a theoretical standpoint. This work investigates how transformers learn to solve symbolic multi-step reasoning problems through chain-of-thought processes, focusing on path-finding in trees. We analyze two intertwined tasks: a backward reasoning task, where the model outputs a path from a goal node to the root, and a more complex forward reasoning task, where the model implements two-stage reasoning by first identifying the goal-to-root path and then reversing it to produce the root-to-goal path. Our theoretical analysis, grounded in the dynamics of gradient descent, shows that trained one-layer transformers can provably solve both tasks with generalization guarantees to unseen trees. In particular, our multi-phase training dynamics for forward reasoning elucidate how different attention heads learn to specialize and coordinate autonomously to solve the two subtasks in a single autoregressive path. These results provide a mechanistic explanation of how trained transformers can implement sequential algorithmic procedures. Moreover, they offer insights into the emergence of reasoning abilities, suggesting that when tasks are structured to take intermediate chain-of-thought steps, even shallow multi-head transformers can effectively solve problems that would otherwise require deeper architectures.

papers.title: Do Transformers know symbolic rules, and would we know if they did?
papers.research_question: Do Transformers internalize genuine symbolic rules, and how can we distinguish symbolic rule use from associative pattern matching?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that Transformers may function as the processor component within a larger symbolic architecture that uses input and output as external memory, and experimentally shows that generalization for abstract rules is significantly stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in classification tasks.
papers.conclusion: The question of whether Transformers internalize symbolic rules remains open, but the full input-Transformer-output pipeline can satisfy the architectural criterion of symbolicity by using attention and positional encoding for location-based memory addressing.
papers.key_findings:
T5 demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization across vocabularies in all tested tasks.
In vocabulary flip settings, T5 completely fails at classification tasks without data mixing, but achieves moderate success in sequence-to-sequence tasks even without mixing.
Repetition detection remains difficult for T5 even with mixed data, indicating a specific obstacle to learning abstract rules when associative heuristics are unavailable.
Generalization is systematically stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in comparable classification tasks.
The results highlight the challenge of conclusively attributing symbolic rule internalization to Transformers due to the unfalsifiability of non-symbolic explanations.
papers.limitation:
The experimental setup is simple and artificial, using artificial vocabularies of single characters and restricting the model architecture to T5.
The classification tasks are restricted to binary targets, and experiments are limited to a single Transformer variant.
future_direction: Examine the performance of tokens with more prevalent linguistic functions and compare different linguistic classes and languages in multilingual models.
Expand experiments to multi-class and multi-label settings, and to more Transformer variants and hyperparameters.
Investigate whether non-symbolic associative explanations for zero-shot success on identical token detection are plausible in practice.
papers.abstract: To improve the explainability of leading Transformer networks used in NLP, it is important to tease apart genuine symbolic rules from merely associative input-output patterns. However, we identify several inconsistencies in how ``symbolicity'' has been construed in recent NLP literature. To mitigate this problem, we propose two criteria to be the most relevant, one pertaining to a system's internal architecture and the other to the dissociation between abstract rules and specific input identities. From this perspective, we critically examine prior work on the symbolic capacities of Transformers, and deem the results to be fundamentally inconclusive for reasons inherent in experiment design. We further maintain that there is no simple fix to this problem, since it arises -- to an extent -- in all end-to-end settings. Nonetheless, we emphasize the need for more robust evaluation of whether non-symbolic explanations exist for success in seemingly symbolic tasks. To facilitate this, we experiment on four sequence modelling tasks on the T5 Transformer in two experiment settings: zero-shot generalization, and generalization across class-specific vocabularies flipped between the training and test set. We observe that T5's generalization is markedly stronger in sequence-to-sequence tasks than in comparable classification tasks. Based on this, we propose a thus far overlooked analysis, where the Transformer itself does not need to be symbolic to be part of a symbolic architecture as the processor, operating on the input and output as external memory components.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Circuit Transformer: A Transformer That Preserves Logical Equivalence
papers.research_question: Can generative neural models (like Transformers) be used for circuit realization while strictly preserving logical equivalence?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Circuit Transformer, a generative neural model that generates logic circuits strictly equivalent to a given Boolean function, using a decoding mechanism with cutoff properties to preserve equivalence throughout generation.
papers.conclusion: The Circuit Transformer is effective for equivalence-preserving circuit generation and optimization, demonstrating strong performance on synthetic and real benchmarks without violating equivalence constraints.
papers.key_findings:
The Circuit Transformer generates equivalent circuits without any violation of equivalence constraints.
It outperforms existing neural approaches on circuit size minimization for both synthetic and real benchmarks.
The decoding mechanism with cutoff properties ensures logical equivalence is preserved during step-by-step generation.
The method can be formulated as a Markov decision process for circuit optimization, allowing search within the equivalence class.
papers.limitation: The current representation may lead to long sequences for nodes with many outgoing edges, and a more compact representation is left for future work.
future_direction: Including additional types of gates in the vocabulary.
Developing a more compact representation for circuits with many outgoing edges.
papers.abstract: Implementing Boolean functions with circuits consisting of logic gates is fundamental in digital computer design. However, the implemented circuit must be exactly equivalent, which hinders generative neural approaches on this task due to their occasionally wrong predictions. In this study, we introduce a generative neural model, the "Circuit Transformer", which eliminates such wrong predictions and produces logic circuits strictly equivalent to given Boolean functions. The main idea is a carefully designed decoding mechanism that builds a circuit step-by-step by generating tokens, which has beneficial "cutoff properties" that block a candidate token once it invalidate equivalence. In such a way, the proposed model works similar to typical LLMs while logical equivalence is strictly preserved. A Markov decision process formulation is also proposed for optimizing certain objectives of circuits. Experimentally, we trained an 88-million-parameter Circuit Transformer to generate equivalent yet more compact forms of input circuits, outperforming existing neural approaches on both synthetic and real world benchmarks, without any violation of equivalence constraints.

papers.title: Seq-VCR: Preventing Collapse in Intermediate Transformer Representations for Enhanced Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers limit reasoning capabilities, and can a regularization technique prevent this collapse to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Seq-VCR, a regularization technique that prevents representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers, and shows that combining it with pause tokens improves reasoning performance without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate layer representation collapse detrimentally affects the computation of intermediate information essential for solving arithmetic reasoning tasks, and Seq-VCR enhances the model's representation capacity to improve its ability to solve these tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Seq-VCR prevents representation collapse and increases entropy in intermediate transformer layers.
Seq-VCR combined with pause tokens achieves 99.5% exact match accuracy on 5x5 digit multiplication, outperforming same-size models (0%) and GPT-4 with CoT (44%).
Seq-VCR improves performance on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets.
Representation collapse is identified as a key factor limiting transformer reasoning capabilities.
Seq-VCR enables models to solve complex reasoning tasks without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.limitation: Pause tokens share the same embedding, which may limit their effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore the effect of having different embeddings per pause token.
Enhance pre-training with improved representation learning to increase model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only Transformers often struggle with complex reasoning tasks, particularly arithmetic reasoning requiring multiple sequential operations. In this work, we identify representation collapse in the model's intermediate layers as a key factor limiting their reasoning capabilities. To address this, we propose Sequential Variance-Covariance Regularization (Seq-VCR), which enhances the entropy of intermediate representations and prevents collapse. Combined with dummy pause tokens as substitutes for chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, our method significantly improves performance in arithmetic reasoning problems. In the challenging $5 \times 5$ integer multiplication task, our approach achieves $99.5\%$ exact match accuracy, outperforming models of the same size (which yield $0\%$ accuracy) and GPT-4 with five-shot CoT prompting ($44\%$). We also demonstrate superior results on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets. Our findings highlight the importance of preventing intermediate layer representation collapse to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Transformers and show that Seq-VCR offers an effective solution without requiring explicit CoT supervision.

papers.title: Systematic Generalization and Emergent Structures in Transformers Trained on Structured Tasks
papers.research_question: How and when can transformers acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization on algorithmic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Two-layer causal transformers with label-based order encoding can learn algorithmic tasks and generalize to longer sequences, exhibiting signs of task decomposition and shared computation across tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve structured algorithmic tasks and generalize systematically, with attention layers developing task decomposition and shared computation.
papers.key_findings:
Label-based order encoding enables strong length generalization in transformers on algorithmic tasks.
Two-layer transformers are sufficient to solve multi-level sorting tasks, while single-layer models fail.
Attention patterns in two-layer models show task decomposition: first layer attends to items in the same feature group, second layer attends to the next output token.
In multi-task learning, transformers can learn multiple tasks simultaneously and generalize to longer sequences, with attention heads showing shared computation across tasks.
Task-conditioned item representations are reorganized according to the task structure, showing clustering by relevant features.
papers.limitation:
Label-based encoding alone would not represent true item distance information.
The tasks are simple and synthetic, and may not capture the complexity of natural data.
future_direction: Explore learning and generalization dynamics in transformer-based agents to understand the acquisition of task-conditioned, multi-level behavioral policies in structured environments.
Characterize the degree of possible computational modularity in multi-headed attention in relation to task structures.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks have seen great success in natural language processing and machine vision, where task objectives such as next word prediction and image classification benefit from nuanced context sensitivity across high-dimensional inputs. However, there is an ongoing debate about how and when transformers can acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization. Here, we explore how well a causal transformer can perform a set of algorithmic tasks, including copying, sorting, and hierarchical compositions of these operations. We demonstrate strong generalization to sequences longer than those used in training by replacing the standard positional encoding typically used in transformers with labels arbitrarily paired with items in the sequence. We search for the layer and head configuration sufficient to solve these tasks, then probe for signs of systematic processing in latent representations and attention patterns. We show that two-layer transformers learn reliable solutions to multi-level problems, develop signs of task decomposition, and encode input items in a way that encourages the exploitation of shared computation across related tasks. These results provide key insights into how attention layers support structured computation both within a task and across multiple tasks.

papers.title: The Kinetics of Reasoning: How Chain-of-Thought Shapes Learning in Transformers?
papers.research_question: How does chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision affect the learning dynamics and generalization of transformers on formal reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: CoT supervision accelerates generalization in transformers on certain reasoning tasks and can be modeled by a kinetic framework, but it also reveals a transient phase of unfaithfulness where answers are correct but reasoning traces are not.
papers.conclusion: CoT supervision advances the take-off point and often raises the ceiling of generalization, but it also reveals a transient faithfulness gap. Mechanistic analyses show that CoT shifts computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
CoT generally improves task performance but its benefits depend on task complexity.
CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections.
There is a transient trace unfaithfulness phase where models produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps.
CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically, shifting computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
Learning curves for both CoT and non-CoT training can be described by a predictable logistic function in log training steps.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic reasoning tasks used are different from real-world reasoning tasks, and the setup does not assess how natural language understanding (i.e., large-scale pretraining) affects CoT reasoning.
The study uses a fixed-size transformer architecture; extending the study to different model sizes could provide more insights on whether model scale affects the learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision can substantially improve transformer performance, yet the mechanisms by which models learn to follow and benefit from CoT remain poorly understood. We investigate these learning dynamics through the lens of grokking by pretraining transformers on symbolic reasoning tasks with tunable algorithmic complexity and controllable data composition to study their generalization. Models were trained under two settings: (i) producing only final answers, and (ii) emitting explicit CoT traces before answering. Our results show that while CoT generally improves task performance, its benefits depend on task complexity. To quantify these effects, we model the accuracy of the logarithmic training steps with a three-parameter logistic curve, revealing how the learning speed and shape vary with task complexity, data distribution, and the presence of CoT supervision. We also uncover a transient trace unfaithfulness phase: early in training, models often produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps, before later aligning their reasoning traces with answers. Empirically, we (1) demonstrate that CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections; (2) introduce a kinetic modeling framework for understanding transformer learning; (3) characterize trace faithfulness as a dynamic property that emerges over training; and (4) show CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically.

papers.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
papers.research_question: This paper investigates when and how Transformer models can learn algorithms that generalize to longer input lengths than seen during training, focusing on length generalization in algorithmic tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the RASP-Generalization Conjecture, which predicts that Transformers length generalize on a task if the task can be solved by a short RASP program that works for all input lengths. It validates this conjecture experimentally and uses it to improve generalization on hard tasks like parity and addition.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the RASP conjecture provides a unifying framework for understanding length generalization in Transformers, offering a novel perspective on the mechanisms of compositional generalization and the algorithmic capabilities of Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers exhibit strong length generalization on tasks that can be solved by short RASP-L programs.
The RASP-Generalization Conjecture captures most known instances of length generalization on algorithmic tasks.
Using insights from RASP-L, the authors drastically improve length generalization performance on traditionally hard tasks such as parity and addition.
The paper provides a theoretical example where the 'min-degree-interpolator' model does not correctly predict Transformers' out-of-distribution behavior, but the RASP conjecture does.
The work suggests that algorithms simple to represent in RASP-L are more likely to be learned and generalized by Transformers.
papers.limitation: RASP-L is not complete and may not capture all Transformer-representable algorithms, such as numerical algorithms involving high-dimensional floating-point operations.
future_direction: Developing more formal and precise conjectures about Transformers' implicit bias.
Investigating more refined notions of complexity beyond minimum RASP-L program length.
Extending the framework to compositional generalization beyond length generalization.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit surprising emergent generalization properties, yet also struggle on many simple reasoning tasks such as arithmetic and parity. This raises the question of if and when Transformer models can learn the true algorithm for solving a task. We study the scope of Transformers' abilities in the specific setting of length generalization on algorithmic tasks. Here, we propose a unifying framework to understand when and how Transformers can exhibit strong length generalization on a given task. Specifically, we leverage RASP (Weiss et al., 2021) -- a programming language designed for the computational model of a Transformer -- and introduce the RASP-Generalization Conjecture: Transformers tend to length generalize on a task if the task can be solved by a short RASP program which works for all input lengths. This simple conjecture remarkably captures most known instances of length generalization on algorithmic tasks. Moreover, we leverage our insights to drastically improve generalization performance on traditionally hard tasks (such as parity and addition). On the theoretical side, we give a simple example where the "min-degree-interpolator" model of learning from Abbe et al. (2023) does not correctly predict Transformers' out-of-distribution behavior, but our conjecture does. Overall, our work provides a novel perspective on the mechanisms of compositional generalization and the algorithmic capabilities of Transformers.

papers.title: Diversity of Transformer Layers: One Aspect of Parameter Scaling Laws
papers.research_question: How do the internal layer dynamics (specifically the diversity of layer outputs) in Transformers relate to parameter scaling laws?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that diversity of predictions from each module in the Transformer residual stream is crucial for performance, and that adding layers improves performance only when layers are diverse, with diminishing returns that align with parameter scaling laws.
papers.conclusion: The diversity of predictions from each module on the residual stream is important for improving Transformer performance, and the effectiveness of adding layers diminishes as the number of layers increases, consistent with parameter scaling laws.
papers.key_findings:
Performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse.
Diversity becomes especially critical when individual layers' outputs are far from the ground truth.
Adding layers enhances performance only when those layers behave differently (are diverse).
The performance gains from increasing layers exhibit submodularity: marginal improvements diminish as additional layers increase, mirroring the logarithmic convergence predicted by parameter scaling laws.
Experiments on multiple semantic-understanding tasks with various LLMs empirically confirm these theoretical properties.
papers.limitation: The decomposition based on mean squared error (MSE) is specific to logits, and there may be a gap when targeting tasks that use softmax to obtain probability, such as uncertainty estimation, confidence calibration, and beam decoding. Furthermore, using information-theoretic diversity for actual tasks requires calculating the probability density of the representation on the residual stream, which is difficult without approximation or assumptions.
papers.abstract: Transformers deliver outstanding performance across a wide range of tasks and are now a dominant backbone architecture for large language models (LLMs). Their task-solving performance is improved by increasing parameter size, as shown in the recent studies on parameter scaling laws. Although recent mechanistic-interpretability studies have deepened our understanding of the internal behavior of Transformers by analyzing their residual stream, the relationship between these internal mechanisms and the parameter scaling laws remains unclear. To bridge this gap, we focus on layers and their size, which mainly decide the parameter size of Transformers. For this purpose, we first theoretically investigate the layers within the residual stream through a bias-diversity decomposition. The decomposition separates (i) bias, the error of each layer's output from the ground truth, and (ii) diversity, which indicates how much the outputs of each layer differ from each other. Analyzing Transformers under this theory reveals that performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse. We show that diversity becomes especially critical when individual layers' outputs are far from the ground truth. Finally, we introduce an information-theoretic diversity and show our main findings that adding layers enhances performance only when those layers behave differently, i.e., are diverse. We also reveal the performance gains from increasing the number of layers exhibit submodularity: marginal improvements diminish as additional layers increase, mirroring the logarithmic convergence predicted by the parameter scaling laws. Experiments on multiple semantic-understanding tasks with various LLMs empirically confirm the theoretical properties derived in this study.

papers.title: Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: Does Huginn exhibit signs of latent chain-of-thought reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: We find limited evidence of interpretable latent chain-of-thought reasoning in the depth-recurrent transformer Huginn-3.5B, and uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks.
papers.conclusion: We find little evidence of structured latent chain-of-thought reasoning in Huginn, but it may be more subtle or distributed than our tools can detect.
papers.key_findings:
Probing inconsistencies across blocks in Huginn's depth-recurrent architecture: hidden state interpretability depends heavily on block index and decoding method.
Token rank trajectory analysis provides little evidence for latent CoT reasoning.
Scaling recurrence depth fails to match explicit reasoning: increasing recurrent steps only marginally improves performance and falls short of explicit CoT prompting.
papers.limitation: The results do not definitively rule out the presence of latent CoT; it may be more subtle or distributed than our employed tools can detect.
future_direction: Apply more advanced probing techniques, such as activation patching, to uncover finer-grained reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has enabled transformer-based language models to excel at complex mathematics and multi-step planning. However, in standard decoder-only architectures, these reasoning steps are externalized in natural language, improving interpretability at the cost of efficiency. To capture reasoning that is not easily represented in words, many works have explored recurrent architectures that aim to internalize reasoning in latent space, potentially supporting latent CoT. In this paper, we investigate whether such reasoning structures emerge in Huginn-3.5B, a depth-recurrent Transformer that reuses layers at inference time without increasing parameter count. We examine the model's internal behavior on arithmetic tasks using a suite of probing techniques including the Logit Lens and Coda Lens. Our findings reveal limited evidence of interpretable latent CoT by tracking rank trajectories of final and intermediate result tokens. Furthermore, we uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks, where the interpretability of hidden states depends heavily on both the layer index and the decoding method. Finally, we empirically show that increasing recurrence depth yields only marginal gains and falls well short of models that explicitly externalize reasoning steps. The code is available at https://github.com/wenquanlu/huginn-latent-cot.

papers.title: Transformer Layers as Painters
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether transformer layers share a common representation space, whether they are all necessary, whether middle layers perform the same function, and the impact of reordering, skipping, or parallelizing layers on model performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that middle transformer layers share a common representation space and are robust to reordering, skipping, or parallel execution, enabling accuracy-latency trade-offs without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies three classes of layers in transformers, with middle layers sharing a common representation and showing uniformity but not redundancy, and finds that execution order is more critical for reasoning tasks than semantic tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers share a common representation space, while the first and last few layers are distinct.
Transformers are robust to skipping middle layers, with performance degrading gracefully.
Middle layers are not redundant; sharing weights among them causes catastrophic performance drop.
Reversing or randomizing the order of middle layers leads to graceful degradation, with random order performing better than reverse.
Running layers in parallel works well except for math-heavy tasks, and looping parallelized layers further improves performance.
papers.limitation:
The painter analogy is not a rigorous theory.
A full explanation for why transformers are robust to the variations is left for future work.
Experiments are conducted primarily on frozen models; fine-tuning might yield different results.
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of layer behaviors in transformer architectures.
Investigating the effect of fine-tuning on the variations.
Testing the variations on models without residual connections.
papers.abstract: Despite their nearly universal adoption for large language models, the internal workings of transformers are not well understood. We aim to better understand the impact of removing or reorganizing information throughout the layers of a pretrained transformer. Such an understanding could both yield better usage of existing models as well as to make architectural improvements to produce new variants. We present a series of empirical studies on frozen models that show that the lower and final layers of pretrained transformers differ from middle layers, but that middle layers have a surprising amount of uniformity. We further show that some classes of problems have robustness to skipping layers, running the layers in an order different from how they were trained, or running the layers in parallel. Our observations suggest that even frozen pretrained models may gracefully trade accuracy for latency by skipping layers or running layers in parallel.

papers.title: Case-Based or Rule-Based: How Do Transformers Do the Math?
papers.research_question: Whether transformers use rule-based or case-based reasoning for math problems.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows transformers use case-based reasoning for math problems and proposes Rule-Following Fine-Tuning (RFFT) to teach them rule-based reasoning, which improves length generalization.
papers.conclusion: Transformers perform case-based reasoning for math problems, but can be taught to use rule-based reasoning via RFFT, leading to better generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers rely on case-based reasoning for math problems, even when using scratchpad.
Intervention experiments (Leave-Square-Out) show performance drops when similar training cases are removed, confirming case-based reasoning.
Rule-Following Fine-Tuning (RFFT) enables transformers to perform rule-based reasoning by explicitly providing and following rules.
RFFT significantly improves length generalization for addition, allowing models trained on 1-5 digit addition to generalize to up to 12 digits with high accuracy.
In-context learning also exhibits characteristics of case-based reasoning, where similar examples in the context contribute more than random ones.
papers.limitation:
RFFT is a task-specific method and requires carefully designed input-output sequences.
The work mainly focuses on fine-tuning models for specific tasks, not on exploring the reasoning mechanism of pre-trained models.
future_direction: Exploring how various prompting techniques (e.g., CoT, least-to-most prompting) affect case-based vs. rule-based reasoning.
Extending RFFT to more tasks and exploring its application to pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance in a variety of complex tasks, modern large language models (LLMs) still have trouble dealing with some math problems that are simple and intuitive for humans, such as addition. While we can easily learn basic rules of addition and apply them to new problems of any length, LLMs struggle to do the same. Instead, they may rely on similar cases seen in the training corpus for help. We define these two different reasoning mechanisms as "rule-based reasoning" and "case-based reasoning". Since rule-based reasoning is essential for acquiring systematic generalization ability, we aim to explore exactly whether transformers use rule-based or case-based reasoning for math problems. Through carefully designed intervention experiments on five math tasks, we confirm that transformers are performing case-based reasoning, no matter whether scratchpad is used, which aligns with the previous observations that transformers use subgraph matching/shortcut learning to reason. To mitigate such problems, we propose a Rule-Following Fine-Tuning (RFFT) technique to teach transformers to perform rule-based reasoning. Specifically, we provide explicit rules in the input and then instruct transformers to recite and follow the rules step by step. Through RFFT, we successfully enable LLMs fine-tuned on 1-5 digit addition to generalize to up to 12-digit addition with over 95% accuracy, which is over 40% higher than scratchpad. The significant improvement demonstrates that teaching LLMs to use rules explicitly helps them learn rule-based reasoning and generalize better in length.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Assessing Logical Reasoning Capabilities of Encoder-Only Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Can encoder-only transformer models perform logical reasoning tasks? How general is this ability, and which layers contribute most?
papers.core_contribution: Encoder-only transformer models can be trained to perform logical reasoning tasks but do not acquire general logical reasoning capabilities; they learn dataset-specific features instead.
papers.conclusion: Encoder-only transformer models do not possess robust logical reasoning capabilities; they learn dataset-specific features during fine-tuning, and the knowledge is localized in higher layers.
papers.key_findings:
Encoder-only transformer models can be fine-tuned to classify logical hypotheses with reasonable accuracy on various datasets.
Pretrained RoBERTa-large has very limited or no intrinsic logical reasoning abilities.
Fine-tuned models show limited transferability across datasets, indicating they learn dataset-specific statistical features rather than general reasoning.
Layerwise probing reveals that higher layers are primarily responsible for solving the hypothesis classification task.
The knowledge necessary for logical reasoning emerges in higher layers and is not transferable, suggesting a lack of robust logical capabilities.
papers.limitation: The analysis focused on RoBERTa-large for cross-probing and layerwise experiments, and conclusions may not extend to other encoder-only models or decoder models.
future_direction: Explore other encoder-only models and decoder/encoder-decoder models
Analyze other representations like attentions and feedforward computations
Investigate other logical formalisms beyond propositional calculus and first-order logic
papers.abstract: Logical reasoning is central to complex human activities, such as thinking, debating, and planning; it is also a central component of many AI systems as well. In this paper, we investigate the extent to which encoder-only transformer language models (LMs) can reason according to logical rules. We ask whether those LMs can deduce theorems in propositional calculus and first-order logic; if their relative success in these problems reflects general logical capabilities; and which layers contribute the most to the task. First, we show for several encoder-only LMs that they can be trained, to a reasonable degree, to determine logical validity on various datasets. Next, by cross-probing fine-tuned models on these datasets, we show that LMs have difficulty in transferring their putative logical reasoning ability, which suggests that they may have learned dataset-specific features, instead of a general capability. Finally, we conduct a layerwise probing experiment, which shows that the hypothesis classification task is mostly solved through higher layers.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: Achieving and Understanding Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Systematic Reasoning in Small-Scale Transformers
papers.research_question: How do small-scale transformers achieve out-of-distribution generalization in systematic reasoning tasks, specifically using Sudoku puzzles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that out-of-distribution generalization in systematic reasoning can be achieved in small-scale transformers by training on component tasks sampled from the full distribution, and that sensitivity to absolute positional encoding can impede generalization, which can be overcome with alternative encoding methods.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can achieve out-of-distribution generalization in systematic reasoning when trained on component tasks with full distribution coverage and with positional encoding schemes that reduce reliance on absolute positions, but further research is needed to understand few-shot learning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A single forward pass is insufficient for learning the Hidden Single strategy; sequential, multi-step reasoning is necessary.
Including training examples on Full House and Naked Single subtasks allows the model to exhibit substantial out-of-distribution generalization for the Hidden Single strategy.
Models struggle to generalize to held-out digits due to over-reliance on absolute token positions in the input sequence.
Padding the input sequences to align token positions can improve digit generalization, but this approach is impractical for general use.
Using positional encoding methods that suppress sensitivity to absolute positions, such as ALiBi and SRL, enables effective out-of-distribution generalization to held-out digits.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to small-scale transformers and synthetic Sudoku tasks, which may not generalize to larger models or more naturalistic datasets.
The model's reliance on absolute positional encoding impedes generalization, highlighting a deficiency in current approaches.
future_direction: Explore the hypothesis of component task coverage in larger and more naturalistic datasets.
Investigate corrections for deficiencies related to positional encoding to improve generalization in larger models.
papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution generalization (OODG) is a longstanding challenge for neural networks. This challenge is quite apparent in tasks with well-defined variables and rules, where explicit use of the rules could solve problems independently of the particular values of the variables, but networks tend to be tied to the range of values sampled in their training data. Large transformer-based language models have pushed the boundaries on how well neural networks can solve previously unseen problems, but their complexity and lack of clarity about the relevant content in their training data obfuscates how they achieve such robustness. As a step toward understanding how transformer-based systems generalize, we explore the question of OODG in small scale transformers trained with examples from a known distribution. Using a reasoning task based on the puzzle Sudoku, we show that OODG can occur on a complex problem if the training set includes examples sampled from the whole distribution of simpler component tasks. Successful generalization depends on carefully managing positional alignment when absolute position encoding is used, but we find that suppressing sensitivity to absolute positions overcomes this limitation. Taken together our results represent a small step toward understanding and promoting systematic generalization in transformers.

papers.title: An explainable transformer circuit for compositional generalization
papers.research_question: How does a compact transformer achieve compositional induction? What is the underlying circuit responsible for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and mechanistically interprets the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer, and shows that this understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can implement structured and interpretable mechanisms for compositional functions, and disassembling transformer circuitry yields benefits for understanding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of specific attention heads that implement compositional induction, including Output Head, Primitive-Pairing Head, Question-Broadcast Head, RHS-Scanner Head, Primitive-Retrieval Head, and Function-Retrieval Head.
Validated the circuit through causal ablations, showing how index information flows from question to output.
Demonstrated that swapping positional embeddings in the circuit leads to predictable changes in attention patterns, confirming the causal role of the circuit.
Provided a program-like description of the algorithm implemented by the transformer circuit.
Showed that the circuit encodes both index-in-question and relative-index-on-LHS information, which are matched in the Output Head's QK alignment.
papers.limitation:
The circuit analysis focused on a relatively small transformer; it is unclear if similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
The techniques required substantial human effort (path-patching, ablations, interpretation); for large-scale models, manual approaches become less feasible.
Targeted activation swaps only partially perturb the model's behavior due to the distributed nature of the mechanism; complete perturbation requires coordinating interventions across multiple heads.
future_direction: Investigating whether similar interpretable circuits exist in larger models.
Developing automated or semi-automated methods for circuit discovery and interpretation to reduce human effort.
Creating systematic workflows for coordinating interventions across all heads to achieve complete perturbation.
papers.abstract: Compositional generalization-the systematic combination of known components into novel structures-remains a core challenge in cognitive science and machine learning. Although transformer-based large language models can exhibit strong performance on certain compositional tasks, the underlying mechanisms driving these abilities remain opaque, calling into question their interpretability. In this work, we identify and mechanistically interpret the circuit responsible for compositional induction in a compact transformer. Using causal ablations, we validate the circuit and formalize its operation using a program-like description. We further demonstrate that this mechanistic understanding enables precise activation edits to steer the model's behavior predictably. Our findings advance the understanding of complex behaviors in transformers and highlight such insights can provide a direct pathway for model control.

papers.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) help transformers recover a world model in the form of finite state automata (FSAs), or do they merely learn shortcuts?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer+CoT learns implicit finite state automata (FSAs) for state tracking, as evidenced by mechanistic analysis showing that late-layer MLP neurons implement state transitions and exhibit compression and distinction properties.
papers.conclusion: Transformer+CoT achieves near-perfect next-token prediction while internalizing an FSA-like structured state representation, bridging the gap between theoretical expressiveness and practical learnability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer+CoT efficiently learns state tracking for sequences of arbitrary length across multiple groups (Z60, A4 × Z5, A5), outperforming other architectures like RNNs and transformer variants.
The circuit for state tracking relies heavily on late-layer MLP neurons, with MLP11 playing a key role.
Neurons in late-layer MLPs can be classified into states based on transition rules with high accuracy, indicating an N-to-1 mapping between neurons and states.
The model exhibits near-perfect compression and distinction metrics, providing evidence that it recovers an implicit FSA structure.
The learned FSAs are robust to skipping intermediate steps and noise in scratchpads, but struggle with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
papers.limitation: The model struggles with generalization to significantly longer sequences.
future_direction: Modifications to model architecture, loss functions, or optimization algorithms to improve length generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks, and prior research shows that CoT can theoretically increase expressiveness. However, there is limited mechanistic understanding of the algorithms that Transformer+CoT can learn. Our key contributions are: (1) We evaluate the state tracking capabilities of Transformer+CoT and its variants, confirming the effectiveness of CoT. (2) Next, we identify the circuit (a subset of model components, responsible for tracking the world state), indicating that late-layer MLP neurons play a key role. We propose two metrics, compression and distinction, and show that the neuron sets for each state achieve nearly 100% accuracy, providing evidence of an implicit finite state automaton (FSA) embedded within the model. (3) Additionally, we explore three challenging settings: skipping intermediate steps, introducing data noises, and testing length generalization. Our results demonstrate that Transformer+CoT learns robust algorithms (FSAs), highlighting its resilience in challenging scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/IvanChangPKU/FSA.

papers.title: Change of Thought: Adaptive Test-Time Computation
papers.research_question: How can we boost the expressive power of encoder Transformers without resorting to token-level autoregression?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the SELF-Transformer, an encoder layer that iteratively refines its own attention weights to a fixed point, enabling adaptive test-time computation and improving performance without increasing parameter count.
papers.conclusion: SELF-Transformer recovers much of the expressive power of iterative reasoning while preserving the simplicity of pure encoder architectures, demonstrating substantial benefits from input-adaptive alignment at test time.
papers.key_findings:
SELF-Transformer achieves up to 20% accuracy gains on encoder-style benchmarks without increasing parameter count.
On the induction head task, SELF-Transformer achieves 91.1% accuracy compared to 63.1% for a standard Transformer.
On language benchmarks (GLUE, SQuAD, WikiText2), SELF-Transformer outperforms baseline models like BERT-base and RoBERTa-base.
On image classification (ImageNet-1K), SELF-ViT achieves 86.3% top-1 accuracy, outperforming ViT and EfficientNet-B7.
On vision-language tasks, SELF-VLTransformer achieves competitive performance on VQA and retrieval tasks.
papers.limitation:
Computational overhead can arise if the fixed-point iteration requires a high number of steps.
Need for further investigation on generalization capabilities and scaling properties across a wider array of complex tasks, deeper architectures, and longer sequences.
The current implementation does not directly return the iteration count for incorporating an explicit ponder cost for regularization.
future_direction: Adaptation and integration of SELF attention into Large Language Models (LLMs).
Development of more computationally efficient fixed-point solvers and advanced convergence control strategies.
Moving towards explicit and learnable pondering schemes and deeper theoretical understanding of the iterative process.
papers.abstract: Transformers evaluated in a single, fixed-depth pass are provably limited in expressive power to the constant-depth circuit class TC0. Running a Transformer autoregressively removes that ceiling -- first in next-token prediction and, more recently, in chain-of-thought reasoning. Both regimes rely on feedback loops that decode internal states into tokens only to re-encode them in subsequent steps. While this "thinking aloud" mirrors human reasoning, biological brains iterate without externalising intermediate states as language. To boost the expressive power of encoder Transformers without resorting to token-level autoregression, we introduce the SELF-Transformer: an encoder layer that iteratively refines its own attention weights to a fixed point. Instead of producing -- in one pass -- the alignment matrix that remixes the input sequence, the SELF-Transformer iteratively updates that matrix internally, scaling test-time computation with input difficulty. This adaptivity yields up to 20\% accuracy gains on encoder-style benchmarks without increasing parameter count, demonstrating that input-adaptive alignment at test time offers substantial benefits for only a modest extra compute budget. Self-Transformers thus recover much of the expressive power of iterative reasoning while preserving the simplicity of pure encoder architectures.

papers.title: Unlocking Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Transformers via Recursive Latent Space Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the architectural mechanisms and inductive biases needed for robust OOD algorithmic generalization in Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces four architectural mechanisms (input-adaptive recurrence, algorithmic supervision, discrete latent space, error correction) that enable Transformers to achieve robust out-of-distribution generalization on a mathematical reasoning task, and provides mechanistic interpretability analysis of the learned circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an architectural approach for native latent-space reasoning in Transformer networks, demonstrating robust algorithmic generalization capabilities and providing insights through mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Standard chain-of-thought training enables limited out-of-distribution generalization but performance degrades rapidly beyond the training distribution.
The proposed four mechanisms (recurrence, algorithmic supervision, discretization, error correction) enable perfect generalization to inputs several times larger than those seen during training.
Mechanistic interpretability reveals that the model learns circuits for variable copying in the first attention layer and value copying in the second attention layer.
The second layer MLP performs modular addition in the frequency domain, amplifying diagonal frequency components that encode the sum.
The discrete latent space anchors representations to a common space, preventing representational shift and facilitating scaling.
papers.limitation: The model does not perform self-correction when trained on perfect data.
future_direction: Training the model with corrupted data to enable self-correction
papers.abstract: Systematic, compositional generalization beyond the training distribution remains a core challenge in machine learning -- and a critical bottleneck for the emergent reasoning abilities of modern language models. This work investigates out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in Transformer networks using a GSM8K-style modular arithmetic on computational graphs task as a testbed. We introduce and explore a set of four architectural mechanisms aimed at enhancing OOD generalization: (i) input-adaptive recurrence; (ii) algorithmic supervision; (iii) anchored latent representations via a discrete bottleneck; and (iv) an explicit error-correction mechanism. Collectively, these mechanisms yield an architectural approach for native and scalable latent space reasoning in Transformer networks with robust algorithmic generalization capabilities. We complement these empirical results with a detailed mechanistic interpretability analysis that reveals how these mechanisms give rise to robust OOD generalization abilities.

papers.title: Attention as a Hypernetwork
papers.research_question: What mechanisms underlie compositional generalization in transformers? The paper investigates whether multi-head attention can be viewed as a hypernetwork and if this perspective explains compositional generalization.
papers.core_contribution: The paper reformulates multi-head attention as a hypernetwork, showing that attention scores across heads form a latent code that specifies operations and is reused for compositional generalization. Introducing a nonlinear value network (HYLA) improves compositional generalization.
papers.conclusion: The hypernetwork perspective provides a useful framework for understanding compositional generalization in transformers, and strengthening this mechanism via a nonlinear value network (HYLA) improves compositional generalization on abstract reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-head attention can be equivalently expressed as a linear hypernetwork that configures key-query specific computations via a latent code formed by attention scores across heads.
The latent code is predictive of the subtasks the network performs and shows structured clusters corresponding to task components (e.g., fuzzy logic terms or SRAVEN rules).
Scaling model size and data enables compositional generalization on abstract reasoning tasks like SRAVEN.
Modifying attention to have a nonlinear value network (HYLA) improves compositional generalization compared to standard softmax and linear attention.
Ablating the hypernetwork mechanism (e.g., using a single head) hurts compositional generalization, supporting the hypernetwork perspective.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to models trained from scratch, and it is unclear if large pretrained models exhibit similar latent code structure.
future_direction: Investigating whether large pretrained models form a similarly structured latent code.
Exploring other levels of granularity for the hypernetwork parameterization and different pooling operators in multi-head attention.
Connecting the hypernetwork perspective to attention-based graph neural networks.
papers.abstract: Transformers can under some circumstances generalize to novel problem instances whose constituent parts might have been encountered during training, but whose compositions have not. What mechanisms underlie this ability for compositional generalization? By reformulating multi-head attention as a hypernetwork, we reveal that a composable, low-dimensional latent code specifies key-query specific operations. We find empirically that this latent code is predictive of the subtasks the network performs on unseen task compositions, revealing that latent codes acquired during training are reused to solve unseen problem instances.
