To further examine the hypothesis that the intrinsic hypernetwork of multi-head attention supports compositional generalization, we ablate whether making the hypernetwork-generated linear value network nonlinear strengthens compositionality. We find that this modification improves compositional generalization on abstract reasoning tasks. In particular, we introduce a symbolic version of the Raven's Progressive Matrices human intelligence test, which gives us precise control over the problem compositions encountered during training and evaluation. We demonstrate on this task how scaling model size and data enables compositional generalization in transformers and gives rise to a functionally structured latent space.

papers.title: On the Computational Power of Transformers and Its Implications in Sequence Modeling
papers.research_question: What is the computational power of Transformers as captured by Turing-completeness, and which components are necessary for this power?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides alternate proofs that vanilla Transformers and directional Transformers (with positional masking only) are Turing-complete, and analyzes the necessity of various components for this completeness.
papers.conclusion: The class of languages recognized by Transformers and RNNs are exactly the same, implying that differences in performance arise from learning abilities rather than computational power.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla Transformers are Turing-complete.
Directional Transformers (with positional masking and no explicit positional encodings) are also Turing-complete.
The decoder-encoder attention block is necessary for Turing-completeness.
The residual connection around the decoder-encoder attention block is necessary for Turing-completeness.
The feedforward network in the decoder is necessary for Turing-completeness.
papers.limitation: The proofs rely on arbitrary precision, which is not practical as implementations use fixed precision.
future_direction: Study of Transformers in finite precision settings.
papers.abstract: Transformers are being used extensively across several sequence modeling tasks. Significant research effort has been devoted to experimentally probe the inner workings of Transformers. However, our conceptual and theoretical understanding of their power and inherent limitations is still nascent. In particular, the roles of various components in Transformers such as positional encodings, attention heads, residual connections, and feedforward networks, are not clear. In this paper, we take a step towards answering these questions. We analyze the computational power as captured by Turing-completeness. We first provide an alternate and simpler proof to show that vanilla Transformers are Turing-complete and then we prove that Transformers with only positional masking and without any positional encoding are also Turing-complete. We further analyze the necessity of each component for the Turing-completeness of the network; interestingly, we find that a particular type of residual connection is necessary. We demonstrate the practical implications of our results via experiments on machine translation and synthetic tasks.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Inner Loop Inference for Pretrained Transformers: Unlocking Latent Capabilities Without Training
papers.research_question: Is it possible to add refinement steps at inference time to improve model performance without changing model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes inference-time inner looping, a method to extend computation in frozen pretrained Transformers by re-applying a selected block range, leading to modest accuracy gains across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Inference-time inner looping offers a lightweight way to expose depth-limited latent computation in off-the-shelf Transformers, further confirming the logits refinement hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Naive inner looping causes distribution shift and performance degradation.
Regularization methods like uniform interpolation enable stable inner looping.
Inner looping yields modest accuracy gains for Gemma models across reasoning benchmarks.
Llama 3-8B is less responsive to inner looping, likely due to its pre-norm architecture.
Visualization of latent trajectories indicates small perturbations that affect final logits.
papers.limitation: The method yields only modest improvements and is less effective on pre-norm architectures like Llama 3-8B.
papers.abstract: Deep Learning architectures, and in particular Transformers, are conventionally viewed as a composition of layers. These layers are actually often obtained as the sum of two contributions: a residual path that copies the input and the output of a Transformer block. As a consequence, the inner representations (i.e. the input of these blocks) can be interpreted as iterative refinement of a propagated latent representation. Under this lens, many works suggest that the inner space is shared across layers, meaning that tokens can be decoded at early stages. Mechanistic interpretability even goes further by conjecturing that some layers act as refinement layers. Following this path, we propose inference-time inner looping, which prolongs refinement in pretrained off-the-shelf language models by repeatedly re-applying a selected block range. Across multiple benchmarks, inner looping yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements. Analyses of the resulting latent trajectories suggest more stable state evolution and continued semantic refinement. Overall, our results suggest that additional refinement can be obtained through simple test-time looping, extending computation in frozen pretrained models.

papers.title: Beyond Components: Singular Vector-Based Interpretability of Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: Can transformer components (attention heads and MLPs) be decomposed into orthogonal singular directions that reveal superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a directional interpretability perspective that decomposes transformer components into orthogonal singular directions, showing that multiple low-rank, interpretable computations coexist within single attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed, opening new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of learned singular directions can faithfully preserve model behavior.
These directions align with meaningful subfunctions, e.g., in IOI, name mover heads encode multiple overlapping subfunctions along distinct singular directions.
Components identified as part of known circuits exhibit strong engagement along specific singular directions, indicating computations are embedded in compact subspaces.
Transformer computations are distributed, structured, and compositional, with overlapping subfunctions embedded within shared subspaces.
Singular directions can be used for controlled interventions, e.g., in gender pronoun resolution, scaling directions can modify predictions.
papers.limitation: Some directions remain challenging to interpret fully.
future_direction: Conduct targeted intervention experiments to validate causal contributions of discovered components.
Examine whether these mechanisms generalize to larger or more capable models (e.g., Phi, LLaMA).
Explore activation of these mechanisms in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit complex and distributed behavior, yet their internal computations remain poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability methods typically treat attention heads and multilayer perceptron layers (MLPs) (the building blocks of a transformer architecture) as indivisible units, overlooking possibilities of functional substructure learned within them. In this work, we introduce a more fine-grained perspective that decomposes these components into orthogonal singular directions, revealing superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP. We validate our perspective on widely used standard tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Gender Pronoun (GP), and Greater Than (GT), showing that previously identified canonical functional heads, such as the name mover, encode multiple overlapping subfunctions aligned with distinct singular directions. Nodes in a computational graph, that are previously identified as circuit elements show strong activation along specific low-rank directions, suggesting that meaningful computations reside in compact subspaces. While some directions remain challenging to interpret fully, our results highlight that transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed. This perspective opens new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability and a deeper understanding of model internals.

papers.title: Disentangling and Integrating Relational and Sensory Information in Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: How can we improve relational reasoning in Transformer architectures by explicitly disentangling and integrating sensory and relational information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Dual Attention Transformer (DAT), an architectural extension that introduces separate sensory and relational attention mechanisms, leading to improved data and parameter efficiency across diverse tasks.
papers.conclusion: Integrating explicit relational attention mechanisms into the Transformer architecture improves performance and efficiency across a range of tasks, including relational reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, image recognition, and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
DAT is more sample-efficient than standard Transformers on synthetic relational reasoning tasks.
DAT outperforms standard Transformers on mathematical problem-solving tasks across model sizes.
DAT achieves higher accuracy than standard Vision Transformers on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image classification.
DAT language models achieve lower perplexity than standard Transformers on the FineWeb-Edu dataset.
papers.abstract: Relational reasoning is a central component of generally intelligent systems, enabling robust and data-efficient inductive generalization. Recent empirical evidence shows that many existing neural architectures, including Transformers, struggle with tasks requiring relational reasoning. In this work, we distinguish between two types of information: sensory information about the properties of individual objects, and relational information about the relationships between objects. While neural attention provides a powerful mechanism for controlling the flow of sensory information between objects, the Transformer lacks an explicit computational mechanism for routing and processing relational information. To address this limitation, we propose an architectural extension of the Transformer framework that we call the Dual Attention Transformer (DAT), featuring two distinct attention mechanisms: sensory attention for directing the flow of sensory information, and a novel relational attention mechanism for directing the flow of relational information. We empirically evaluate DAT on a diverse set of tasks ranging from synthetic relational benchmarks to complex real-world tasks such as language modeling and visual processing. Our results demonstrate that integrating explicit relational computational mechanisms into the Transformer architecture leads to significant performance gains in terms of data efficiency and parameter efficiency.

papers.title: Do Language Models Use Their Depth Efficiently?
papers.research_question: Do deeper language models use their depth to compose more features for higher-order computations, or do they merely spread the same kinds of computation out over more layers?
papers.core_contribution: Deeper language models do not use their increased depth to learn new kinds of computation; instead, they spread the same computation over more layers and use the second half primarily for fine-grained refinement of the output probability distribution.
papers.conclusion: Current large language models underutilize the second half of their layers, which may explain why increasing depth leads to diminishing returns in performance for stacked Transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in the second half of the model contribute much less to the residual stream than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition around the middle.
Skipping layers in the second half has a much smaller effect on future computations and output predictions compared to skipping layers in the first half.
For multi-hop tasks, there is no evidence that models use increased depth to compose sub-results; later computation steps do not use more layers.
Linear maps from a shallow model's residual stream to a deeper model's show a diagonal pattern, indicating the deeper model 'stretches out' the same computation rather than performing novel computation.
The second half of the network is devoted to refining the current token's probability distribution, not computing reusable sub-results for future tokens.
papers.limitation:
The findings are a case study on Llama and Qwen models and may not hold for other model types.
The work does not answer how models solve problems without depth dependence.
The linear map analysis in Section 3.4 relies on a single model pair due to resource constraints.
The exploration in Section 3.5 relies on manual study of individual trained models.
future_direction: Develop an automatic metric to measure the correspondence of computation to the parse tree.
Verify the findings with more resources on different and deeper models.
Investigate how models solve problems without depth dependence.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs are increasingly deep, and depth correlates with performance, albeit with diminishing returns. However, do these models use their depth efficiently? Do they compose more features to create higher-order computations that are impossible in shallow models, or do they merely spread the same kinds of computation out over more layers? To address these questions, we analyze the residual stream of the Llama 3.1, Qwen 3, and OLMo 2 family of models. We find: First, comparing the output of the sublayers to the residual stream reveals that layers in the second half contribute much less than those in the first half, with a clear phase transition between the two halves. Second, skipping layers in the second half has a much smaller effect on future computations and output predictions. Third, for multihop tasks, we are unable to find evidence that models are using increased depth to compose subresults in examples involving many hops. Fourth, we seek to directly address whether deeper models are using their additional layers to perform new kinds of computation. To do this, we train linear maps from the residual stream of a shallow model to a deeper one. We find that layers with the same relative depth map best to each other, suggesting that the larger model simply spreads the same computations out over its many layers. All this evidence suggests that deeper models are not using their depth to learn new kinds of computation, but only using the greater depth to perform more fine-grained adjustments to the residual. This may help explain why increasing scale leads to diminishing returns for stacked Transformer architectures.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Quantifying LLM Attention-Head Stability: Implications for Circuit Universality
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn the same internal representations across different training runs, specifically focusing on the stability of attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically quantifies the stability of attention heads across different training runs of transformer language models, finding that middle-layer heads are least stable, weight decay improves stability, and the residual stream is more stable, with implications for circuit universality in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The findings establish that cross-instance robustness of circuits is an essential prerequisite for scalable oversight, highlighting the importance of stability in interpretability for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Middle-layer attention heads are the least stable across refits and the most representationally distinct.
Deeper models exhibit stronger mid-depth divergence in attention head stability.
Unstable heads in deeper layers become more functionally important than their peers.
Using AdamW optimizer with weight decay substantially improves attention-head stability across refits.
The residual stream is comparatively more stable than attention heads across refits.
papers.limitation: CKA can underestimate similarity when refits differ by transformations outside its scope, potentially affecting residual stream stability comparisons.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models and different architectures.
Investigate stability patterns in vision transformers or other modalities.
Explore the effect of different training regimes or data distributions on stability.
papers.abstract: In mechanistic interpretability, recent work scrutinizes transformer "circuits" - sparse, mono or multi layer sub computations, that may reflect human understandable functions. Yet, these network circuits are rarely acid-tested for their stability across different instances of the same deep learning architecture. Without this, it remains unclear whether reported circuits emerge universally across labs or turn out to be idiosyncratic to a particular estimation instance, potentially limiting confidence in safety-critical settings. Here, we systematically study stability across-refits in increasingly complex transformer language models of various sizes. We quantify, layer by layer, how similarly attention heads learn representations across independently initialized training runs. Our rigorous experiments show that (1) middle-layer heads are the least stable yet the most representationally distinct; (2) deeper models exhibit stronger mid-depth divergence; (3) unstable heads in deeper layers become more functionally important than their peers from the same layer; (4) applying weight decay optimization substantially improves attention-head stability across random model initializations; and (5) the residual stream is comparatively stable. Our findings establish the cross-instance robustness of circuits as an essential yet underappreciated prerequisite for scalable oversight, drawing contours around possible white-box monitorability of AI systems.

papers.title: How Do Transformers Learn Variable Binding in Symbolic Programs?
papers.research_question: How do Transformers learn variable binding and dereferencing in symbolic programs without built-in symbolic operations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn systematic variable binding and dereferencing without explicit architectural support, evolving through a three-phase developmental trajectory where the final solution builds upon earlier heuristics rather than replacing them.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to implement fundamental aspects of symbolic computation, like variable binding, through learned mechanisms that use the residual stream as addressable memory, bridging connectionist and symbolic approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The model's learning trajectory has three distinct phases: random prediction of numbers, shallow heuristics (prioritizing early lines), and finally a systematic dereferencing mechanism.
The model learns to use its residual stream as an addressable memory space, with specialized attention heads routing information across token positions to track variable assignments.
The final systematic mechanism builds upon and coexists with earlier-learned heuristics, challenging narratives that networks discard simple strategies.
The model develops separate, linearly decodable subspaces within the residual stream for numerical constants and variable names.
The model generalizes well to longer programs and more hops than seen in training for cases not solvable by its early-line heuristics.
papers.limitation:
The model's generalization is limited for programs where the correct answer is on the first line when program length varies, as it relies on a line-1 heuristic that fails to generalize.
Linear probing suggests the model does not maintain a complete, linearly decodable program state representation, indicating a more dynamic, routing-based strategy.
papers.abstract: Variable binding -- the ability to associate variables with values -- is fundamental to symbolic computation and cognition. Although classical architectures typically implement variable binding via addressable memory, it is not well understood how modern neural networks lacking built-in binding operations may acquire this capacity. We investigate this by training a Transformer to dereference queried variables in symbolic programs where variables are assigned either numerical constants or other variables. Each program requires following chains of variable assignments up to four steps deep to find the queried value, and also contains irrelevant chains of assignments acting as distractors. Our analysis reveals a developmental trajectory with three distinct phases during training: (1) random prediction of numerical constants, (2) a shallow heuristic prioritizing early variable assignments, and (3) the emergence of a systematic mechanism for dereferencing assignment chains. Using causal interventions, we find that the model learns to exploit the residual stream as an addressable memory space, with specialized attention heads routing information across token positions. This mechanism allows the model to dynamically track variable bindings across layers, resulting in accurate dereferencing. Our results show how Transformer models can learn to implement systematic variable binding without explicit architectural support, bridging connectionist and symbolic approaches. To facilitate reproducible research, we developed Variable Scope, an interactive web platform for exploring our findings at https://variablescope.org

papers.title: Lessons on Parameter Sharing across Layers in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can parameter sharing across layers in Transformers be made more efficient than the Universal Transformer approach, which shares one layer's parameters across all layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes parameter sharing strategies (SEQUENCE, CYCLE, CYCLE(REV)) that relax the strict sharing of Universal Transformers, achieving better computational efficiency and comparable or better performance across multiple tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed parameter sharing strategies are efficient in terms of parameter size and computational time, and are effective alternatives to Universal Transformers across various sequence-to-sequence tasks and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed strategies achieve slightly better BLEU scores than Universal Transformers with smaller computational time when using the same parameter size.
The proposed strategies outperform Universal Transformers under the same computational budgets (same training time).
The strategies are effective in high-resource machine translation settings, other language pairs, and automatic speech recognition.
In language modeling, the proposed strategies (especially SEQUENCE) outperform both the vanilla Transformer and Universal Transformer.
The best strategy (SEQUENCE, CYCLE, or CYCLE(REV)) may depend on the task and Transformer architecture (Post-LN vs. Pre-LN).
papers.limitation:
Lacks theoretical justifications for the proposed parameter sharing strategies.
Did not conduct experiments on the pre-training and then fine-tuning configuration (e.g., like BERT) due to computational budget limitations.
It is difficult to conclude which of the three strategies is best because performance depends on the task and Transformer architecture.
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of the training dynamics to understand the relation between parameter sharing strategies and Transformer architectures.
Investigating the effectiveness of the proposed strategies in pre-training and fine-tuning configurations.
Investigating the performance in more realistic situations, e.g., combining with parameter-efficient embedding methods.
papers.abstract: We propose a parameter sharing method for Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017). The proposed approach relaxes a widely used technique, which shares parameters for one layer with all layers such as Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019), to increase the efficiency in the computational time. We propose three strategies: Sequence, Cycle, and Cycle (rev) to assign parameters to each layer. Experimental results show that the proposed strategies are efficient in the parameter size and computational time. Moreover, we indicate that the proposed strategies are also effective in the configuration where we use many training data such as the recent WMT competition.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Binary and Ternary Transformers
papers.research_question: Do binary and ternary transformer networks learn distinctly different or similar algorithms compared to full-precision transformer networks for modular addition?
papers.core_contribution: Binary and ternary transformers learn similar Fourier-based algorithms as full-precision transformers for modular addition, providing evidence against their use as more interpretable alternatives.
papers.conclusion: Binary and ternary transformers learn similar algorithms to full-precision transformers for modular addition and are not more interpretable, with binary models showing more noise in analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Binary and ternary networks exhibit grokking behavior similar to full-precision networks when weight decay regularization is applied.
Binary and ternary models learn similar periodic patterns in embeddings and logits as full-precision models.
Binary models show more noise in Fourier analysis compared to full-precision models.
Ternary models behave intermediately between binary and full-precision models but do not achieve superior loss.
No evidence was found that binary or ternary networks learn simpler, more interpretable discrete algorithms.
papers.limitation:
Lack of conclusive evidence concerning exactly what algorithm was learned, since many different algorithms could be learned for modular addition.
The implementation did not binarize/ternarize the embed and unembed layers, limiting the study to partially binarized networks.
Only the most basic straight-through estimator technique was explored for optimizing binary/ternary networks.
future_direction: Explore more complicated techniques for optimizing binary and ternary networks using mechanistic interpretability.
Investigate fully binarized/ternarized networks in all layers.
Investigate whether binary and ternary networks always learn similar algorithms for other toy problems or in language models.
papers.abstract: Recent research (arXiv:2310.11453, arXiv:2402.17764) has proposed binary and ternary transformer networks as a way to significantly reduce memory and improve inference speed in Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining accuracy. In this work, we apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to investigate whether such networks learn distinctly different or similar algorithms when compared to full-precision transformer networks. In particular, we reverse engineer the algorithms learned for the toy problem of modular addition where we find that binary and ternary networks learn similar algorithms as full precision networks. This provides evidence against the possibility of using binary and ternary networks as a more interpretable alternative in the LLM setting.

papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers is Reasoning through Shortcuts
papers.research_question: Why does advanced reasoning capability fail to emerge in implicit reasoning? How do language models perform implicit reasoning in multi-step mathematical tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Language models acquire implicit reasoning through shortcut learning, which enables strong performance on tasks with similar patterns but lacks generalization, especially in the 'Variable as Subtrahend Plight'.
papers.conclusion: Language models rely on shortcuts for implicit reasoning, which only work when training data aligns with a specific pattern, and they struggle when true reasoning is required.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform step-by-step implicit reasoning and generalize to longer steps when trained on fixed-pattern data.
When trained on unfixed-pattern data, models overfit to shortcuts and fail to generalize, particularly in cases with variables as subtrahends.
State-of-the-art LLMs also rely on shortcuts for implicit reasoning and struggle with variable subtrahends, indicating the generality of the shortcut learning phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Only two fundamental arithmetic operators are used, limiting the scope of mathematical reasoning studied.
Evaluation of LLMs may be inflated if they were exposed to similar synthetic tasks during training.
future_direction: Expand to include a broader range of mathematical operators.
Explore reasoning beyond arithmetic problems, e.g., commonsense reasoning.
papers.abstract: Test-time compute is emerging as a new paradigm for enhancing language models' complex multi-step reasoning capabilities, as demonstrated by the success of OpenAI's o1 and o3, as well as DeepSeek's R1. Compared to explicit reasoning in test-time compute, implicit reasoning is more inference-efficient, requiring fewer generated tokens. However, why does the advanced reasoning capability fail to emerge in the implicit reasoning style? In this work, we train GPT-2 from scratch on a curated multi-step mathematical reasoning dataset and conduct analytical experiments to investigate how language models perform implicit reasoning in multi-step tasks. Our findings reveal: 1) Language models can perform step-by-step reasoning and achieve high accuracy in both in-domain and out-of-domain tests via implicit reasoning. However, this capability only emerges when trained on fixed-pattern data. 2) Conversely, implicit reasoning abilities emerging from training on unfixed-pattern data tend to overfit a specific pattern and fail to generalize further. Notably, this limitation is also observed in state-of-the-art large language models. These findings suggest that language models acquire implicit reasoning through shortcut learning, enabling strong performance on tasks with similar patterns while lacking generalization.

papers.title: Deconstructing Attention: Investigating Design Principles for Effective Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Which design principles of dot-product attention are essential for effective language modeling, and can some be relaxed in hybrid architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Token mixing is indispensable for language modeling, while the mathematical form and sequence dependency can be relaxed, especially in hybrid architectures where standard attention layers stabilize simpler variants.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that token mixing is essential, but other attention principles can be simplified, especially when standard attention layers are interleaved, leading to robust performance.
papers.key_findings:
Token mixing is crucial; without it, models perform near-random on NLU tasks.
The standard mathematical form is important in uniform configurations but can be relaxed in hybrid ones.
Sequence-dependency enhances generalization ability.
Current QK derivation is not as essential as expected.
Layer collaboration allows poor-performing variants to contribute in hybrid architectures.
papers.limitation: Experiments are limited to models up to 500M parameters, 15B tokens pretraining, and monolingual tokenizer.
future_direction: Experimenting with larger models and different model families.
papers.abstract: The success of Transformer language models is widely credited to their dot-product attention mechanism, which interweaves a set of key design principles: mixing information across positions (enabling multi-token interactions), sequence-dependent activations (where attention weights adapt to each input), a specific mathematical form (dot-product similarities plus softmax weighting), and coupling of queries and keys to evolving hidden states (grounding attention in the current layer). However, the necessity of each of these principles remains largely untested. In this work, we systematically deconstruct attention by designing controlled variants that selectively relax these principles, applied both uniformly across all layers and in hybrid architectures where only some layers retain standard attention. Our empirical analysis reveals that mechanisms for mixing tokens are indispensable, as their absence collapses models to near-random behavior, while the exact mathematical form and sequence dependency can be substantially relaxed, especially when preserved in just a subset of layers. Surprisingly, even variants that fail in isolation can achieve robust performance when interleaved with standard attention, highlighting a cooperative effect. These findings deepen our understanding of what truly underpins attention's effectiveness and open new avenues for simplifying language models without sacrificing performance.

papers.title: Characterizing Intrinsic Compositionality in Transformers with Tree Projections
papers.research_question: Does the transformer learn a tree-like computation when trained on language data, and how can we measure its tree-structuredness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised, parameter-free method to functionally project transformers into tree-structured networks, showing that transformers become more tree-like during training and that tree-structuredness predicts compositional generalization.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results suggest that making further progress on human-like compositional generalization might require inductive biases that encourage the emergence of latent tree-like structure.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers become more tree-like over training on sequence transduction tasks.
Tree projections sometimes align with gold syntax.
Induced trees reflect contextual dependence structure.
Tree-structuredness correlates better with compositional generalization than in-domain accuracy.
Self-supervised training does not lead to tree-like computation in low data regimes.
papers.abstract: When trained on language data, do transformers learn some arbitrary computation that utilizes the full capacity of the architecture or do they learn a simpler, tree-like computation, hypothesized to underlie compositional meaning systems like human languages? There is an apparent tension between compositional accounts of human language understanding, which are based on a restricted bottom-up computational process, and the enormous success of neural models like transformers, which can route information arbitrarily between different parts of their input. One possibility is that these models, while extremely flexible in principle, in practice learn to interpret language hierarchically, ultimately building sentence representations close to those predictable by a bottom-up, tree-structured model. To evaluate this possibility, we describe an unsupervised and parameter-free method to \emph{functionally project} the behavior of any transformer into the space of tree-structured networks. Given an input sentence, we produce a binary tree that approximates the transformer's representation-building process and a score that captures how "tree-like" the transformer's behavior is on the input. While calculation of this score does not require training any additional models, it provably upper-bounds the fit between a transformer and any tree-structured approximation. Using this method, we show that transformers for three different tasks become more tree-like over the course of training, in some cases unsupervisedly recovering the same trees as supervised parsers. These trees, in turn, are predictive of model behavior, with more tree-like models generalizing better on tests of compositional generalization.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Transformers as Multi-task Learners: Decoupling Features in Hidden Markov Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformers achieve multi-task generalization? Specifically, what are the layerwise mechanisms by which they represent and process sequential information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers learn local features in lower layers and decoupled, temporally disentangled features in upper layers when modeling Hidden Markov Models, and provides theoretical constructions that align with these observations.
papers.conclusion: This work advances theoretical and empirical understanding of how Transformers achieve strong generalization across sequence learning tasks, showing they transition from local feature learning in lower layers to decoupled representations in upper layers, providing a principled explanation for their expressiveness and efficiency in multi-task and in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Well-trained Transformers achieve high accuracy under in-context learning on HMMs, with performance improving as more input-output examples are provided or as sequence length increases.
Lower layers of Transformers focus on learning local representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens.
Upper layers develop decoupled, temporally disentangled representations that are less tied to specific input positions and encode higher-level abstractions.
Transformers gradually recognize task identity across layers, with hidden state identification occurring earlier than task identification, indicating a layerwise processing hierarchy.
The theoretical construction demonstrates that Transformers can approximate low-rank HMMs using a fixed-length memory structure, enabling effective in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Analysis is limited to Hidden Markov Models and may not generalize to more complex settings.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more general assumptions and more complex model settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer based models have shown remarkable capabilities in sequence learning across a wide range of tasks, often performing well on specific task by leveraging input-output examples. Despite their empirical success, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. In this work, we investigate the layerwise behavior of Transformers to uncover the mechanisms underlying their multi-task generalization ability. Taking explorations on a typical sequence model, i.e, Hidden Markov Models, which are fundamental to many language tasks, we observe that: first, lower layers of Transformers focus on extracting feature representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens; second, on the upper layers, features become decoupled, exhibiting a high degree of time disentanglement. Building on these empirical insights, we provide theoretical analysis for the expressiveness power of Transformers. Our explicit constructions align closely with empirical observations, providing theoretical support for the Transformer's effectiveness and efficiency on sequence learning across diverse tasks.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Latent Concept Disentanglement in Transformer-based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do transformers represent latent structures when performing in-context learning? Do they disentangle and compose latent concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that transformers disentangle and compose latent concepts during in-context learning, representing them in low-dimensional subspaces that reflect the geometry of the latent parameters.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of disentangling and composing latent concepts during in-context learning, with internal representations that capture the geometry of the underlying latent parameters.
papers.key_findings:
For multi-hop reasoning tasks, the model uses step-by-step composition of latent concepts via a sparse set of attention heads.
The bridge-resolving mechanism is much stronger in the larger 27B model compared to the 2B model, indicating model size benefits latent concept disentanglement.
Adding more in-context examples strengthens the causal importance of the relevant sub-circuits and increases concept representation disentanglement.
For numerical tasks with latent parameters, task vectors lie on low-dimensional smooth manifolds that reflect the geometry of the underlying parameter (e.g., radius).
Interpolating along the task vector manifold allows steering the model's computation, approximately interpolating the latent parameter.
papers.limitation:
Only English language queries are used, so mechanisms may differ across languages.
The latent concepts tested are all human-interpretable (e.g., numbers, countries), limiting generalization to more intricate relationships.
papers.abstract: When large language models (LLMs) use in-context learning (ICL) to solve a new task, they must infer latent concepts from demonstration examples. This raises the question of whether and how transformers represent latent structures as part of their computation. Our work experiments with several controlled tasks, studying this question using mechanistic interpretability. First, we show that in transitive reasoning tasks with a latent, discrete concept, the model successfully identifies the latent concept and does step-by-step concept composition. This builds upon prior work that analyzes single-step reasoning. Then, we consider tasks parameterized by a latent numerical concept. We discover low-dimensional subspaces in the model's representation space, where the geometry cleanly reflects the underlying parameterization. Overall, we show that small and large models can indeed disentangle and utilize latent concepts that they learn in-context from a handful of abbreviated demonstrations.

papers.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
papers.research_question: Does reasoning require large depth but not necessarily many parameters, and can looped models effectively solve reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Looped transformers can solve reasoning tasks with fewer parameters by providing depth through looping, and they exhibit an inductive bias towards reasoning over memorization.
papers.conclusion: Looped models are effective for reasoning tasks, providing depth without many parameters, and have an inductive bias towards improving reasoning performance over memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Looped models nearly match the performance of non-looped models with the same depth on synthetic reasoning tasks like addition, p-hop induction, and i-GSM, despite having fewer parameters.
For language modeling, looped models have worse perplexity but better reasoning performance on downstream tasks compared to non-looped models with the same FLOPs.
Looped models show scaling behavior with effective depth similar to chain-of-thought reasoning.
Theoretically, looped models can simulate iterative algorithms and chain-of-thought reasoning.
A regularization method that encourages layer similarity inherits the inductive bias of looped models towards reasoning.
papers.limitation: The results are limited to the tested reasoning problems and may not generalize to other forms of reasoning (e.g., multimodal and common-sense reasoning).
future_direction: Generalizing the results to other forms of reasoning such as multimodal and common-sense reasoning.
Formalizing reasoning problems more succinctly.
Further exploration of the inductive bias towards reasoning at the same perplexity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have shown remarkable reasoning abilities and scaling laws suggest that large parameter count, especially along the depth axis, is the primary driver. In this work, we make a stronger claim -- many reasoning problems require a large depth but not necessarily many parameters. This unlocks a novel application of looped models for reasoning. Firstly, we show that for many synthetic reasoning problems like addition, $p$-hop induction, and math problems, a $k$-layer transformer looped $L$ times nearly matches the performance of a $kL$-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a $k$-layer model. This is further corroborated by theoretical results showing that many such reasoning problems can be solved via iterative algorithms, and thus, can be solved effectively using looped models with nearly optimal depth. Perhaps surprisingly, these benefits also translate to practical settings of language modeling -- on many downstream reasoning tasks, a language model with $k$-layers looped $L$ times can be competitive to, if not better than, a $kL$-layer language model. In fact, our empirical analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon: looped and non-looped models exhibit scaling behavior that depends on their effective depth, akin to the inference-time scaling of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We further elucidate the connection to CoT reasoning by proving that looped models implicitly generate latent thoughts and can simulate $T$ steps of CoT with $T$ loops. Inspired by these findings, we also present an interesting dichotomy between reasoning and memorization, and design a looping-based regularization that is effective on both fronts.

papers.title: What Can Transformer Learn with Varying Depth? Case Studies on Sequence Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the minimum number of attention layers required for transformers to perform memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization tasks, and what are the roles of different layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a single-layer transformer can memorize but fails at reasoning and generalization; two layers are needed for reasoning and generalization, and three layers may be needed for contextual generalization. It also identifies simple operations that single attention layers can perform and how stacking layers combines them.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that depth is crucial for transformers to perform complex tasks, and their analysis sheds light on how transformers work by combining simple operations.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer transformer can memorize sequences but cannot perform reasoning or generalization tasks.
A two-layer transformer can perform reasoning and generalization tasks.
A three-layer transformer may be needed for contextual generalization.
Single attention layers can perform copying, parsing, matching, and mapping operations; stacking layers combines these to solve complex tasks.
Theoretical proofs and numerical experiments support these findings.
papers.abstract: We study the capabilities of the transformer architecture with varying depth. Specifically, we designed a novel set of sequence learning tasks to systematically evaluate and comprehend how the depth of transformer affects its ability to perform memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization. We show a transformer with only one attention layer can excel in memorization but falls short in other tasks. Then, we show that exhibiting reasoning and generalization ability requires the transformer to have at least two attention layers, while context generalization ability may necessitate three attention layers. Additionally, we identify a class of simple operations that a single attention layer can execute, and show that the complex tasks can be approached as the combinations of these simple operations and thus can be resolved by stacking multiple attention layers. This sheds light on studying more practical and complex tasks beyond our design. Numerical experiments corroborate our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Depths: Dynamically allocating compute in transformer-based language models
papers.research_question: How can transformer-based language models learn to dynamically allocate computational resources (FLOPs) across tokens and layers to improve efficiency without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mixture-of-Depths (MoD), a method for transformers to dynamically allocate a fixed compute budget by learning to route tokens around or through transformer blocks using a top-k mechanism, achieving performance parity or improvement with fewer FLOPs per forward pass and faster inference.
papers.conclusion: Mixture-of-Depths transformers provide a method to dynamically control compute per forward pass, offering a tool for efficient inference and opening doors to extensions like integration with MoE and routing to diverse computational functions.
papers.key_findings:
MoD transformers can match or exceed the performance of isoFLOP-optimal vanilla transformers while using a fraction of the FLOPs per forward pass and being up to 50% faster to step during sampling.
Learned routing is crucial for performance; stochastic routing performs drastically worse.
MoD can be integrated with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) to form MoDE models, where performance improvements compound.
The optimal MoD configuration uses aggressive capacity reduction (e.g., 12.5% of tokens processed per routing block) applied every other block.
An auxiliary loss or predictor enables causal routing during autoregressive sampling with minimal performance degradation, overcoming the non-causal nature of the top-k operation used during training.
future_direction: Decoupling routing decisions for queries, keys, and values in self-attention.
Using routing to implement long-term memory mechanisms where tokens are selectively stored for future retrieval.
Extending routing to choose among diverse computational functions beyond a standard block and a residual connection, such as memory lookup or tool use.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models spread FLOPs uniformly across input sequences. In this work we demonstrate that transformers can instead learn to dynamically allocate FLOPs (or compute) to specific positions in a sequence, optimising the allocation along the sequence for different layers across the model depth. Our method enforces a total compute budget by capping the number of tokens ($k$) that can participate in the self-attention and MLP computations at a given layer. The tokens to be processed are determined by the network using a top-$k$ routing mechanism. Since $k$ is defined a priori, this simple procedure uses a static computation graph with known tensor sizes, unlike other conditional computation techniques. Nevertheless, since the identities of the $k$ tokens are fluid, this method can expend FLOPs non-uniformly across the time and model depth dimensions. Thus, compute expenditure is entirely predictable in sum total, but dynamic and context-sensitive at the token-level. Not only do models trained in this way learn to dynamically allocate compute, they do so efficiently. These models match baseline performance for equivalent FLOPS and wall-clock times to train, but require a fraction of the FLOPs per forward pass, and can be upwards of 50\% faster to step during post-training sampling.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: KV Cache Steering for Controlling Frozen LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we develop lightweight, post-training interventions to unlock and steer inherent reasoning processes in language models, specifically via a one-shot modification of the key-value cache?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cache steering, a one-shot method for steering language model behavior by modifying the key-value cache, which is more efficient and stable than continuous activation steering and does not require fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Cache steering provides a lightweight, practical mechanism for behavior-level guidance of language models, offering a stable and efficient alternative to activation steering and fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Cache steering induces chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models without fine-tuning or prompt modifications.
The method improves reasoning structure and task performance on multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC-c, CSQA, PIQA).
Cache steering is more computationally efficient and stable to hyperparameters than activation steering.
The technique enables controllable transfer of reasoning styles (e.g., stepwise, causal, analogical) from teacher models.
The method scales to larger models and yields gains on challenging datasets like GPQA and MATH.
papers.limitation:
Further study is needed to assess how well cache steering generalizes across a wider range of large models, domains, and tasks beyond reasoning.
Potential misuse, such as steering toward deceptive, harmful, or biased outputs, remains a concern.
future_direction: Further study to assess generalization across a wider range of large models, domains, and tasks beyond reasoning.
papers.abstract: We propose cache steering, a lightweight method for implicit steering of language models via a one-shot intervention applied directly to the key-value cache. To validate its effectiveness, we apply cache steering to induce chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models. Our approach constructs steering vectors from reasoning traces, obtained either from teacher models (e.g., GPT-4o) or existing human annotations, that shift model behavior toward more explicit, multi-step reasoning without fine-tuning or prompt modifications. Experimental evaluations on diverse reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that cache steering improves both the qualitative structure of model reasoning and quantitative task performance. Additional experiments show that the method also scales to larger models and yields further gains on challenging datasets such as GPQA and MATH. Compared to prior activation steering techniques that require continuous interventions, our one-shot cache steering offers substantial advantages in terms of inference latency, hyperparameter stability, and ease of integration with existing inference APIs. Beyond mere reasoning induction, we show that cache steering enables controllable transfer of reasoning styles (e.g., stepwise, causal, analogical), making it a practical tool for behavior-level guidance of language models.

papers.title: It is not True that Transformers are Inductive Learners: Probing NLI Models with External Negation
papers.research_question: Do transformer models fine-tuned on NLI tasks learn to reason logically, specifically with respect to external negation and the law of excluded middle?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models fine-tuned on NLI tasks fail to inductively learn the law of excluded middle for external negation, indicating they do not learn logical reasoning but instead rely on shallow heuristics.
papers.conclusion: Transformer NLI models do not learn logical reasoning with respect to negation, as they fail to inductively learn the law of excluded middle and generalize it to similar prefixes.
papers.key_findings:
Before inoculation, NLI models treat external negation prefixes as distractors, ignoring them and achieving high accuracy only when the number of prefixes is even (which does not change the label).
Many transformer NLI models (DeBERTa and BART) cannot learn to inductively generalize the law of excluded middle even with extensive fine-tuning on challenge data.
Some RoBERTa models can learn the law of excluded middle for a single external negation prefix, but they fail to generalize this pattern to semantically similar prefixes (e.g., from 'it is not true that' to 'it is false that').
Inoculation (fine-tuning) on challenge data leads to catastrophic forgetting, altering the models' representations of negation prefixes and reducing their similarity to related prefixes.
Theorem 1 proves that encoder transformers are theoretically capable of modeling the law of excluded middle for arbitrary external negation prefixes, suggesting the practical failure is due to training procedures or data structure, not architectural limitations.
papers.limitation:
Only encoder and encoder-decoder transformers are considered, not decoder-only models like LLaMa-2 or GPT-3.
Challenge data generation uses only MNLI and SNLI datasets, which may contain non-representative data and annotation artifacts.
Only two external negation prefix triggers ('it is not true that' and 'it is false that') are used, limiting the variety of negation studied.
Theorem 1 applies only to encoder transformers and assumes a fixed input length, which may not fully reflect real-world conditions.
future_direction: Evaluation of decoder-only transformer models (e.g., LLaMa-2, GPT-3) on similar negation tasks.
Incorporating a wider variety of negation triggers in challenge data generation.
Exploring training procedures like unlikelihood with reference training or logic-based regularization to improve negation handling.
papers.abstract: NLI tasks necessitate a substantial degree of logical reasoning; as such, the remarkable performance of SoTA transformers on these tasks may lead us to believe that those models have learned to reason logically.The results presented in this paper demonstrate that (i) models fine-tuned on NLI datasets learn to treat external negation as a distractor, effectively ignoring its presence in hypothesis sentences; (ii) several near-SoTA encoder and encoder-decoder transformer models fail to inductively learn the law of the excluded middle for a single external negation prefix with respect to NLI tasks, despite extensive fine-tuning; (iii) those models which are able to learn the law of the excluded middle for a single prefix are unable to generalize this pattern to similar prefixes.Given the critical role of negation in logical reasoning, we may conclude from these findings that transformers do not learn to reason logically when fine-tuned for NLI tasks.Furthermore, these results suggest that transformers may not be able to inductively learn the role of negation with respect to NLI tasks, calling into question their capacity to fully acquire logical reasoning abilities.

papers.title: On the Computational Power of Transformers and its Implications in\n Sequence Modeling
papers.research_question: What are the computational capabilities of Transformers, specifically regarding Turing-completeness, and which components are necessary for this completeness?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that Transformers with positional masking are Turing-complete, and shows that the decoder-encoder residual connection is necessary for Turing-completeness.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are Turing-complete with either positional encodings or masking; the decoder-encoder residual connection and feedforward network are essential for this completeness.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla Transformers are Turing-complete, providing a simpler proof than prior work.
Transformers with only positional masking (and no positional encoding) are also Turing-complete.
The decoder-encoder attention block is necessary for Turing-completeness.
The residual connection around the decoder-encoder attention block is necessary for Turing-completeness; without it, the model cannot perform tasks requiring inference based on previous outputs.
Experiments show that removing the decoder-encoder residual connection prevents the model from performing counting tasks, but not copy tasks.
papers.limitation: Proofs rely on arbitrary precision, while practical implementations use fixed precision.
future_direction: Study of Transformers in finite precision settings.
papers.abstract:
