papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Extrapolation by Association: Length Generalization Transfer in Transformers
papers.research_question: Can generalization to longer inputs in one task transfer to another task that is only trained on short examples?
papers.core_contribution: Length generalization can be transferred across related tasks in transformers, and this transfer correlates with the reuse of attention heads between tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can transfer length generalization capabilities across related tasks, and this transfer is associated with the reuse of attention heads, highlighting the compositional reuse of inductive structure across tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Length generalization transfers from auxiliary tasks to main tasks when trained jointly, enabling extrapolation to longer inputs.
The transfer effect is strongest when the auxiliary and main tasks are related and when the length ratio is between 0.5 and 2.
Pretraining on natural language improves length generalization transfer in downstream synthetic tasks.
Transfer correlates with shared internal computation, specifically the reuse of attention heads between tasks.
Training dynamics for length generalization transfer are unstable and sensitive to model initialization.
papers.limitation:
Lack of a formal theoretical framework for understanding when and why transfer occurs.
Experiments are limited to relatively simple algorithmic domains with well-defined length parameters and deterministic solution paths.
future_direction: Explore whether similar transfer effects exist for other generalization challenges such as compositional reasoning, distributional shifts, and task complexity.
Investigate transfer in more complex settings involving hierarchical reasoning, abstract problem-solving, or integration of multiple skills.
papers.abstract: Transformer language models have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities in natural language domains, yet we lack a fine-grained understanding of how such generalization arises. In this paper, we investigate length generalization--the ability to extrapolate from shorter to longer inputs--through the lens of \textit{task association}. We find that length generalization can be \textit{transferred} across related tasks. That is, training a model with a longer and related auxiliary task can lead it to generalize to unseen and longer inputs from some other target task. We demonstrate this length generalization transfer across diverse algorithmic tasks, including arithmetic operations, string transformations, and maze navigation. Our results show that transformer models can inherit generalization capabilities from similar tasks when trained jointly. Moreover, we observe similar transfer effects in pretrained language models, suggesting that pretraining equips models with reusable computational scaffolding that facilitates extrapolation in downstream settings. Finally, we provide initial mechanistic evidence that length generalization transfer correlates with the re-use of the same attention heads between the tasks. Together, our findings deepen our understanding of how transformers generalize to out-of-distribution inputs and highlight the compositional reuse of inductive structure across tasks.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Why Can't Transformers Learn Multiplication? Reverse-Engineering Reveals Long-Range Dependency Pitfalls
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication?
papers.core_contribution: By reverse-engineering a successful implicit chain-of-thought model, the paper uncovers that transformers fail at multiplication due to a lack of long-range dependencies, and demonstrates that an auxiliary loss providing the correct inductive bias can enable learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication due to a pitfall in learning long-range dependencies with gradient descent and an auto-regressive loss, but this can be addressed with the correct inductive bias, as demonstrated by the auxiliary loss method.
papers.key_findings:
The ICoT model learns the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication, while standard fine-tuning does not.
The ICoT model encodes long-range dependencies via attention patterns that form a directed acyclic graph (attention tree) to cache and retrieve pairwise partial products.
The ICoT model implements partial products in attention heads as Minkowski sums and represents digits using a Fourier basis, forming an efficient pentagonal prism structure.
Standard fine-tuning converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies, causing loss to plateau on middle digits.
An auxiliary loss that supervises the prediction of a 'running partial sum' via a linear regression probe provides an inductive bias that enables the model to learn multiplication successfully.
papers.limitation: The suggested inductive bias is task-specific and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Developing generalizing inductive biases for tasks with long-range dependencies.
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly capable, yet still fail at a seemingly simple task of multi-digit multiplication. In this work, we study why, by reverse-engineering a model that successfully learns multiplication via \emph{implicit chain-of-thought}, and report three findings: (1) Evidence of long-range structure: Logit attributions and linear probes indicate that the model encodes the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication. (2) Mechanism: the model encodes long-range dependencies using attention to construct a directed acyclic graph to ``cache'' and ``retrieve'' pairwise partial products. (3) Geometry: the model implements partial products in attention heads by forming Minkowski sums between pairs of digits, and digits are represented using a Fourier basis, both of which are intuitive and efficient representations that the standard fine-tuning model lacks. With these insights, we revisit the learning dynamics of standard fine-tuning and find that the model converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies. We further validate this understanding by introducing an auxiliary loss that predicts the ``running sum'' via a linear regression probe, which provides an inductive bias that enables the model to successfully learn multi-digit multiplication. In summary, by reverse-engineering the mechanisms of an implicit chain-of-thought model we uncover a pitfall for learning long-range dependencies in Transformers and provide an example of how the correct inductive bias can address this issue.

papers.title: Layer Specialization Underlying Compositional Reasoning in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers acquire and deploy compositional reasoning skills, and how does layer specialization contribute to this capability?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers develop compositional reasoning through progressive layer specialization, with causal models specializing early layers and masked models specializing late layers, both achieving comparable performance.
papers.conclusion: Transformers develop modular, interpretable mechanisms for compositional reasoning through layer specialization, with architectural constraints shaping where specialization occurs.
papers.key_findings:
Performance improves systematically with task complexity and the number of in-context examples.
Layer specialization emerges during training in three phases: rapid specialization, plateau, and refinement.
Causal models concentrate compositional processing in early layers, while masked models concentrate it in late layers.
Specialization scores correlate with generalization performance, particularly for out-of-distribution tasks.
Both architectures achieve similar out-of-distribution performance despite different specialization strategies.
papers.limitation:
The Random Hierarchy Model is a simplified abstraction of natural language compositionality.
Layer-level analysis provides only a coarse-grained view of computational organization.
Analysis focuses on relatively small models (6 layers).
future_direction: Extending analyses to more naturalistic hierarchical tasks.
Using activation patching or circuit identification for detailed algorithms within specialized layers.
Understanding how specialization patterns evolve with model scale.
papers.abstract: Transformers exhibit compositional reasoning on sequences not observed during training, a capability often attributed to in-context learning (ICL) and skill composition. We investigate this phenomenon using the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), a probabilistic context-free grammar that generates sequences through recursive rule application. Models are trained on subsets of sequences and evaluated across four generalization conditions: memorization, in-distribution generalization, out-of-distribution generalization with the same rules, and cross-layer transfer. Behaviorally, performance improves systematically with task complexity and the number of in-context examples, with out-of-distribution tasks requiring substantially more examples than in-distribution scenarios. Mechanistically, we identify a progressive emergence of layer specialization during training that correlates with generalization performance. Principal component analysis and attention pattern clustering reveal that transformers develop structured, hierarchically organized representations in specialized layers. These results demonstrate that transformers develop modular, interpretable mechanisms supporting compositional reasoning, linking internal algorithmic structure to observed behavioral capabilities.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers
papers.research_question: How can transformer networks be used as programmable computers to emulate complex algorithms and programs by hardcoding them with specific weights and placing them in a loop?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow transformers can be programmed to emulate a general-purpose computer by hardcoding weights and using a loop, enabling them to execute complex algorithms.
papers.conclusion: Even shallow transformers can execute full-fledged, general-purpose programs when programmed with specific weights and placed in a loop, highlighting the versatility of attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
A constant number of transformer layers (up to 13) can emulate basic computing blocks like edit operations, non-linear functions, function calls, program counters, and conditional branches.
Using these building blocks, the transformer can emulate a small instruction-set computer (like SUBLEQ/FLEQ).
The looped transformer can execute programs for a basic calculator, linear algebra operations (matrix inversion, power iteration), and in-context learning algorithms (SGD).
The depth of the transformer does not scale with the program length but only with the complexity of a single instruction.
The attention mechanism is versatile and can be used to implement these operations.
papers.limitation: The way we design our constructions shares no similarities with how real-world language models are trained.
future_direction: Further research into the potential of attention mechanisms and the ability of language models to execute algorithmic instructions.
Determining the minimal transformer network size required to perform specific algorithmic tasks.
Enhancing the capabilities of trained language models by utilizing smaller, reverse-engineered transformer networks for specific algorithmic tasks.
papers.abstract: We present a framework for using transformer networks as universal computers by programming them with specific weights and placing them in a loop. Our input sequence acts as a punchcard, consisting of instructions and memory for data read/writes. We demonstrate that a constant number of encoder layers can emulate basic computing blocks, including embedding edit operations, non-linear functions, function calls, program counters, and conditional branches. Using these building blocks, we emulate a small instruction-set computer. This allows us to map iterative algorithms to programs that can be executed by a looped, 13-layer transformer. We show how this transformer, instructed by its input, can emulate a basic calculator, a basic linear algebra library, and in-context learning algorithms that employ backpropagation. Our work highlights the versatility of the attention mechanism, and demonstrates that even shallow transformers can execute full-fledged, general-purpose programs.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Is Grokking Worthwhile? Functional Analysis and Transferability of Generalization Circuits in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile?
papers.core_contribution: Grokking does not represent genuine acquisition of generalized reasoning; instead, it integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers show limited transferability to novel facts.
papers.conclusion: Grokking merely integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers have limited transferability to novel facts, suggesting a trade-off between data scarcity and computational resources.
papers.key_findings:
Non-grokked and grokked models follow identical reasoning paths on in-distribution compositional queries, indicating that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an established reasoning structure.
Grokking and the formation of a Generalization Circuit are not intrinsically linked; behavioral grokking can occur without circuit formation.
Generalization Circuits exhibit limited transferability; they do not imply full mastery of compositional logic and struggle with new facts in certain positions.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints limit exhaustive exploration of fake grokking due to prolonged training cycles.
Findings are constrained to parameter-sharing Transformer architectures and may not extend to standard transformers.
future_direction: Systematically categorize which data distributions favor circuit formation over pattern memorization.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at factual retrieval, they often struggle with the "curse of two-hop reasoning" in compositional tasks. Recent research suggests that parameter-sharing transformers can bridge this gap by forming a "Generalization Circuit" during a prolonged "grokking" phase. A fundamental question arises: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile? In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study to evaluate the Generalization Circuit's role in knowledge assimilation and transfer. We demonstrate that: (i) The inference paths established by non-grokked and grokked models for in-distribution compositional queries are identical. This suggests that the "Generalization Circuit" does not represent the sudden acquisition of a new reasoning paradigm. Instead, we argue that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an naturally established reasoning path. (ii) Achieving high accuracy on unseen cases after prolonged training and the formation of a certain reasoning path are not bound; they can occur independently under specific data regimes. (iii) Even a mature circuit exhibits limited transferability when integrating new knowledge, suggesting that "grokked" Transformers do not achieve a full mastery of compositional logic.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Dissecting Multiplication in Transformers: Insights into LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do transformers struggle with integer multiplication, and how can their performance be improved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers decompose multiplication into parallel subtasks handled by specialized attention heads, and identifies difficulties with carryover and intermediate results as key limitations. It proposes improvements including reversed answer digits, increased depth, and progressive training, achieving high accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed analysis pipeline elucidates the internal mechanisms of transformers on multiplication tasks and provides targeted improvements, contributing to model interpretability and performance.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers decompose multiplication into parallel subtasks (Base Multiply, Carry, Use Carry, Use Carry and Further Carry) and learn them in a sequential order.
Attention heads specialize in different subtasks; for example, in a 3-head transformer, each head handles a different subtask.
Reversing the order of answer digits improves accuracy by allowing the model to use previously generated digits for carry calculation.
Increasing model depth is necessary to handle multiple intermediate steps in multi-digit multiplication.
Progressive training with a balanced proportion of simple samples (multipliers with only one non-zero digit) improves learning.
future_direction: Analyzing more complex tasks and transformer models
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models have achieved remarkable performance across various natural language processing tasks. However, they often struggle with seemingly easy tasks like arithmetic despite their vast capabilities. This stark disparity raise human's concerns about their safe and ethical use, hinder their widespread adoption.In this paper, we focus on a typical arithmetic task, integer multiplication, to explore and explain the imperfection of transformers in this domain. We provide comprehensive analysis of a vanilla transformer trained to perform n-digit integer multiplication. Our observations indicate that the model decomposes multiplication task into multiple parallel subtasks, sequentially optimizing each subtask for each digit to complete the final multiplication. Based on observation and analysis, we infer the reasons of transformers deficiencies in multiplication tasks lies in their difficulty in calculating successive carryovers and caching intermediate results, and confirmed this inference through experiments. Guided by these findings, we propose improvements to enhance transformers performance on multiplication tasks. These enhancements are validated through rigorous testing and mathematical modeling, not only enhance transformer's interpretability, but also improve its performance, e.g., we achieve over 99.9% accuracy on 5-digit integer multiplication with a tiny transformer, outperform LLMs GPT-4. Our method contributes to the broader fields of model understanding and interpretability, paving the way for analyzing more complex tasks and Transformer models. This work underscores the importance of explainable AI, helping to build trust in large language models and promoting their adoption in critical applications.

papers.title: How do Transformers Learn Implicit Reasoning?
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn implicit reasoning, specifically multi-hop implicit reasoning, and what are the internal mechanisms that enable this ability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory for implicit reasoning in transformers (memorization, in-distribution generalization, cross-distribution generalization) and introduces two diagnostic tools (cross-query semantic patching, cosine-based representational lens) that link representational clustering to reasoning capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit reasoning in transformers is driven by the clustering of intermediate representations in cosine space, and generalization patterns depend on representational alignment, offering insights into the interpretability of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit reasoning emerges in three distinct stages: memorization, in-distribution generalization, and cross-distribution generalization.
Training with atomic triples accelerates learning but is not strictly necessary for in-distribution generalization.
Second-hop generalization requires query-level exposure to specific compositional structures; exposure to the same fact in other roles is insufficient.
Intermediate entity representations are located in middle layers (e.g., layer 5 at the r1 token) and are not necessarily decodable via logit lens, indicating a gap between explicit decodability and functional usage.
Successful reasoning correlates with cosine-space clustering of intermediate representations; generalization patterns depend on representational alignment driven by in-distribution supervision.
papers.limitation: The study uses a controlled symbolic environment, which is simpler than the rich and complex knowledge bases of real LLMs, so the findings are preliminary and may not fully explain reasoning dynamics in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can perform multi-hop reasoning implicitly -- producing correct answers without explicitly verbalizing intermediate steps -- but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we study how such implicit reasoning emerges by training transformers from scratch in a controlled symbolic environment. Our analysis reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory: early memorization, followed by in-distribution generalization, and eventually cross-distribution generalization. We find that training with atomic triples is not necessary but accelerates learning, and that second-hop generalization relies on query-level exposure to specific compositional structures. To interpret these behaviors, we introduce two diagnostic tools: cross-query semantic patching, which identifies semantically reusable intermediate representations, and a cosine-based representational lens, which reveals that successful reasoning correlates with the cosine-base clustering in hidden space. This clustering phenomenon in turn provides a coherent explanation for the behavioral dynamics observed across training, linking representational structure to reasoning capability. These findings provide new insights into the interpretability of implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs, helping to clarify how complex reasoning processes unfold internally and offering pathways to enhance the transparency of such models.

papers.title: LLMCache: Layer-Wise Caching Strategies for Accelerated Reuse in Transformer Inference
papers.research_question: How can transformer inference latency be reduced by reusing intermediate activations from semantically similar inputs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMCache is a layer-wise caching framework that accelerates transformer inference by reusing intermediate activations for semantically similar inputs, achieving up to 3.1× speedup with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.conclusion: LLMCache delivers up to 3.1× speedup in inference time while maintaining task accuracy within a 0.5% margin, providing a practical tool for scalable and efficient language model inference.
papers.key_findings:
LLMCache reduces inference latency by up to 3.1× compared to no caching.
Cache hit rates are higher in lower and mid transformer layers, up to 92%.
Accuracy degradation is less than 0.5% across tasks like WikiText-103, SQuAD v2, and OpenBookQA.
LLMCache outperforms traditional KV caching on GPT-2 models.
The method is model-agnostic and works with both encoder and decoder architectures without retraining.
papers.limitation:
Out-of-Distribution Inputs: In highly variable or unpredictable input domains, fingerprint similarity decreases, leading to lower cache hits.
Memory Scaling: As cache sizes grow, particularly for deeper models, GPU memory management becomes critical.
Fine-Tuning Side Effects: LLMCache assumes stable representations; fine-tuned models with dynamic behavior may experience cache staleness more quickly.
future_direction: Dynamic Thresholding: Adapting similarity threshold per layer or input using a learned uncertainty score.
Distributed Cache Sharing: Sharing cache fingerprints in multi-node serving systems for further reuse benefits.
Learned Fingerprints: Replacing handcrafted hashing with trainable, lightweight embedding encoders.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet their high inference latency poses a significant challenge for real-timeand large-scale deployment. While existing caching mechanisms,such as token-level key-value caches, offer speedups in autore-gressive decoding, they are limited in scope and applicability. In this paper, we present LLMCache, a novel layer-wise caching framework that accelerates transformer inference by reusing intermediate activations based on semantic similarity of input sequences. Unlike prior work, LLMCache is model-agnostic,operates across both encoder and decoder architectures, and supports caching at arbitrary transformer layers. We introduce a lightweight fingerprinting mechanism for matching seman-tically similar inputs and propose adaptive eviction strategies to manage cache staleness. Experiments on BERT and GPT-2 across SQuAD, WikiText-103, and OpenBookQA show up to 3.1 X speedup in inference time with <0.5% accuracy degradation. Our results highlight LLMCache as a practical and general-purpose solution for optimizing transformer inference in real-world applications

papers.title: Autoregressive + Chain of Thought = Recurrent: Recurrence's Role in Language Models' Computability and a Revisit of Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: What are the distinct roles of recurrence and autoregression in neural models' computational power, and how does Chain of Thought (CoT) approximate recurrence to enhance reasoning capabilities in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that recurrence is crucial for computational depth in neural models, and that Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting approximates this missing recurrence in autoregressive Transformers by converting hidden states to text and back, thereby enhancing their computational capabilities. It also introduces the concept of 'recurrence-completeness' to analyze recurrent Transformer variants.
papers.conclusion: The analysis clarifies the roles of autoregression and recurrence, showing recurrence is key for computational depth. CoT approximates recurrence in Transformers, boosting their reasoning. The concept of recurrence-completeness reveals that some recurrent Transformer designs prioritize speed over computational power.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrence, not autoregression, is essential for increasing the depth complexity of neural models, enabling them to solve tasks requiring sequential computation.
Chain of Thought (CoT) mimics recurrence in Transformer-based LLMs by encoding hidden computational states into natural language tokens and decoding them back, acting as a bridge between autoregression and recurrence.
Empirical results show that CoT-enhanced LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) can solve tasks at Regular, Context-Free, and Context-Sensitive computational levels, whereas standard Transformers without CoT fail.
Some 'recurrent' Transformer designs (e.g., Linear Transformer, RWKV) are recurrence-incomplete and do not enhance computational power; they primarily aim for inference efficiency.
There is a trade-off between recurrence-completeness and parallel training: true recurrent models cannot be parallelized, while recurrence-incomplete models like Linear Transformers can.
papers.limitation:
Experimental task lengths are limited to under 20 elements to avoid issues with long-context retrieval and model errors unrelated to computability, which may limit generalizability to longer sequences.
The study uses only one LLM (GPT-4) for experiments, which may not represent all language models.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture excels in a variety of language modeling tasks, outperforming traditional neural architectures such as RNN and LSTM. This is partially due to its elimination of recurrent connections, which allows for parallel training and a smoother flow of gradients. However, this move away from recurrent structures places the Transformer model at the lower end of Chomsky's computational hierarchy, imposing limitations on its computational abilities. Consequently, even advanced Transformer-based models face considerable difficulties in tasks like counting, string reversal, and multiplication. These tasks, though seemingly elementary, require a level of computational complexity that exceeds the capabilities of the Transformer architecture. Concurrently, the emergence of ``Chain of Thought" (CoT) prompting has enabled Transformer-based language models to tackle tasks that were previously impossible or poorly executed. In this work, we thoroughly investigate the influence of recurrent structures in neural models on their reasoning abilities and computability, contrasting the role autoregression plays in the neural models' computational power. We then shed light on how the CoT approach can mimic recurrent computation and act as a bridge between autoregression and recurrence in the context of language models. It is this approximated recurrence that notably improves the model's performance and computational capacity. Moreover, we revisit recent recurrent-based Transformer model designs, focusing on their computational abilities through our proposed concept of ``recurrence-completeness" and identify key theoretical limitations in models like Linear Transformer and RWKV. Through this, we aim to provide insight into the neural model architectures and prompt better model design.

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: AttMEMO : Accelerating Transformers with Memoization on Big Memory Systems
papers.research_question: How can memoization be used to accelerate the self-attention mechanism in transformer model inference without modifying the model architecture or requiring specialized hardware?
papers.core_contribution: AttMemo is a memoization framework that accelerates transformer self-attention inference by reusing similar attention probability matrices, achieving significant latency reduction with negligible accuracy loss.
papers.conclusion: AttMemo successfully accelerates self-attention in transformers using memoization on big memory systems, demonstrating significant performance improvements without model architecture changes or specialized hardware.
papers.key_findings:
There is rich similarity in self-attention computation (specifically in Attention Probability Matrices) across transformer inferences, enabling memoization.
A lightweight MLP embedding model can effectively capture semantic similarity between hidden states to enable efficient search for reusable attention tensors.
Memory mapping eliminates expensive tensor copying during memoization, providing over 500x speedup compared to naive fetching.
Selective memoization guided by a performance model avoids overhead in layers with low similarity, further improving inference time.
AttMemo achieves an average of 22% inference latency reduction (up to 68%) on evaluated transformer models with negligible accuracy loss.
papers.abstract: Transformer models gain popularity because of their superior inference accuracy and inference throughput. However, the transformer is computation-intensive, causing a long inference time. The existing works on transformer inference acceleration have limitations caused by either the modification of transformer architectures or the need of specialized hardware. In this paper, we identify the opportunities of using memoization to accelerate the self-attention mechanism in transformers without the above limitations. Built upon a unique observation that there is rich similarity in attention computation across inference sequences, we build a memoization database that leverages the emerging big memory system. We introduce a novel embedding technique to find semantically similar inputs to identify computation similarity. We also introduce a series of techniques such as memory mapping and selective memoization to avoid memory copy and unnecessary overhead. We enable 22% inference-latency reduction on average (up to 68%) with negligible loss in inference accuracy.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: When Can Transformers Ground and Compose: Insights from Compositional Generalization Benchmarks
papers.research_question: When and how can transformer models ground language to a visual world and generalize compositionally?
papers.core_contribution: Simple transformer-based models (GroCoT) can achieve strong compositional generalization on grounded navigation tasks, and a simplified task (RefEx) reveals that even a single attention layer can ground and compose attributes, with its computations being fully interpretable.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of grounded compositional generalization, with the primary difficulty in existing benchmarks being target identification, and a simplified task (RefEx) allows for a complete interpretation of the model's grounding and compositional reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
GroCoT outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and GSRR benchmarks.
The main challenge in ReaSCAN is target identification, not navigation sequence generation.
The C2 test split in ReaSCAN is unfair; transformers can generalize to deeper structures when trained fairly.
A single self-attention layer with a single head can solve the RefEx task and generalize to novel compositions of object attributes.
The computations of the attention-only transformer on RefEx can be mathematically constructed, providing a complete interpretation of how grounding and composition occur.
papers.abstract: Humans can reason compositionally whilst grounding language utterances to the real world. Recent benchmarks like ReaSCAN use navigation tasks grounded in a grid world to assess whether neural models exhibit similar capabilities. In this work, we present a simple transformer-based model that outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and a modified version of gSCAN. On analyzing the task, we find that identifying the target location in the grid world is the main challenge for the models. Furthermore, we show that a particular split in ReaSCAN, which tests depth generalization, is unfair. On an amended version of this split, we show that transformers can generalize to deeper input structures. Finally, we design a simpler grounded compositional generalization task, RefEx, to investigate how transformers reason compositionally. We show that a single self-attention layer with a single head generalizes to novel combinations of object attributes. Moreover, we derive a precise mathematical construction of the transformer's computations from the learned network. Overall, we provide valuable insights about the grounded compositional generalization task and the behaviour of transformers on it, which would be useful for researchers working in this area.

papers.title: Relational reasoning and inductive bias in transformers and large language models
papers.research_question: How do transformers perform transitive inference, and how do inductive biases differ between in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL) strategies?
papers.core_contribution: IWL naturally induces transitive inference with symbolic distance and terminal item effects, while ICL models develop induction circuits that fail to generalize; however, pre-training on linear regression enables transitive inference in ICL without induction circuits.
papers.conclusion: Both the training regime and the geometric structure of induced representations critically determine transformers' capacity for transitive inference.
papers.key_findings:
IWL models exhibit transitive inference and show symbolic distance and terminal item effects despite training only on adjacent pairs.
ICL models trained only on adjacent pairs fail to generalize and rely on induction circuits implementing match-and-copy strategies.
Pre-training transformers on in-context linear regression tasks enables transitive inference in ICL without forming induction circuits.
Linear geometric prompts improve transitive inference in large language models, while circular prompts impair performance, especially when models cannot rely on stored knowledge.
The advantage of linear over circular prompting increases with model size for incongruent item pairs.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analyses (PCA, ablation studies, attention patterns) were restricted to small transformer architectures for interpretability; internal mechanisms in LLMs remain opaque.
The transitive inference task is a simple example of relational reasoning which might not capture all real-world scenarios.
Results are empirical rather than theoretical.
future_direction: Combine experiments with advanced mechanistic interpretability techniques for LLMs.
Use transitive inference as a benchmark for evaluating model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have demonstrated remarkable reasoning abilities, but the mechanisms underlying relational reasoning remain poorly understood. We investigate how transformers perform \textit{transitive inference}, a classic relational reasoning task which requires inference indirectly related items (e.g., if $A>B$ and $B>C$, then $A>C$), comparing in-weights learning (IWL) and in-context learning (ICL) strategies. We find that IWL naturally induces a generalization bias towards transitive inference despite training only on adjacent items, whereas ICL models develop induction circuits implementing match-and-copy strategies that fail to encode hierarchical relationships. However, when pre-trained on in-context linear regression tasks, transformers successfully exhibit in-context generalizable transitive inference, displaying both \textit{symbolic distance} and \textit{terminal item effects} characteristic of human and animal performance, without forming induction circuits. We extend these findings to large language models, demonstrating that prompting with linear geometric scaffolds improves transitive inference, while circular geometries (which violate transitivity by allowing wraparound) impair performance, particularly when models cannot rely on stored knowledge. Together, these results reveal that both the training regime and the geometric structure of induced representations critically determine transformers' capacity for transitive inference.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can transformers use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') to perform hidden computation and solve algorithmic tasks they cannot solve without intermediate tokens, and under what conditions does this occur?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens to solve hard algorithmic tasks they fail at without intermediate tokens, showing additional tokens provide computational benefits independent of token meaning, but learning to use filler tokens requires specific, dense supervision.
papers.conclusion: For certain parallelizable problems, transformers achieve improved performance with filler tokens instead of chain-of-thought tokens, meaning intermediate tokens can be used purely for computational capacity rather than faithful serial reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve perfect accuracy on 3SUM and high accuracy on 2SUM-Transform with filler tokens, while failing without them.
The performance gap between filler and no-filler settings increases with problem complexity (input length and dimension).
Filler token representations encode hidden, task-relevant computation, as shown by fine-tuning experiments.
Learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires training on parallelizable chain-of-thought data; instance-adaptive CoT data does not transfer.
Filler tokens extend transformer expressive power within the complexity class TC0, enabling solution of problems with deep quantifier nesting.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which token-parallelizable, TC0 algorithmic problems arise in natural language contexts.

Investigate whether natural-language text provides adequate supervision for filler-token computation, providing parallelizable supervision rather than non-parallelizable, instance-adaptive chains of thought.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought responses from language models improve performance across most benchmarks. However, it remains unclear to what extent these performance gains can be attributed to human-like task decomposition or simply the greater computation that additional tokens allow. We show that transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve when responding without intermediate tokens. However, we find empirically that learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge. We also provide a theoretical characterization of the class of problems where filler tokens are useful in terms of the quantifier depth of a first-order formula. For problems satisfying this characterization, chain-of-thought tokens need not provide information about the intermediate computational steps involved in multi-token computations. In summary, our results show that additional tokens can provide computational benefits independent of token choice. The fact that intermediate tokens can act as filler tokens raises concerns about large language models engaging in unauditable, hidden computations that are increasingly detached from the observed chain-of-thought tokens.

papers.title: Carrying over algorithm in transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition, and how are the tasks allocated to different network components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition in a modular fashion, with specific layers handling digit addition, carry decision, and carry addition.
papers.conclusion: Transformers implement the carrying over algorithm in a modular way, and insights from small models can inform understanding of larger models and improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
For two-layer encoder-only models, the carrying over algorithm is implemented modularly with the first layer adding digits, the second layer deciding where to carry, and the MLP adding the carried one.
The same implementation is found in three-layer and decoder-only models.
Suggestive evidence indicates similar mechanisms in large language models like Alpaca 7B, Llemma 7B, and Zephyr 7B.
Length generalization to larger digit sums can be achieved through priming or fine-tuning.
One-layer models exhibit a phase transition in attention patterns during training.
papers.limitation: The evidence for the implementation in large language models is suggestive and not conclusive.
future_direction: Exploring better prompting strategies for large language models
Studying stabilization of attention patterns for length generalization
papers.abstract: Addition is perhaps one of the simplest arithmetic tasks one can think of and is usually performed using the carrying over algorithm. This algorithm consists of two tasks: adding digits in the same position and carrying over a one whenever necessary. We study how transformer models implement this algorithm and how the two aforementioned tasks are allocated to different parts of the network. We first focus on two-layer encoder-only models and show that the carrying over algorithm is implemented in a modular fashion. The first layer is mostly responsible for adding digits in the same position. The second layer first decides, in the attention, which positions need a carried one or not, and then performs the carrying of the one in the final MLP. We provide a simple way of precisely identifying which neurons are responsible for that task. This implementation of the carrying over algorithm occurs across a range of hyperparameters for two as well as three-layer models. For small decoder-only models, we observe the same implementation and provide suggestive evidence for its existence in three 7B large language models.

papers.title: Do Efficient Transformers Really Save Computation?
papers.research_question: Do efficient Transformers (Sparse and Linear Transformers) actually save computation compared to standard Transformers when applied to reasoning tasks modeled as dynamic programming?
papers.core_contribution: Efficient Transformers (Sparse and Linear) require a model size scaling with problem size for general dynamic programming tasks, negating their efficiency gains, but they can be efficient for tasks with a locality assumption.
papers.conclusion: Efficient Transformers do not save computation in general DP tasks due to required model size scaling, but they can be efficient for tasks with locality.
papers.key_findings:
Efficient Transformers are expressive enough to solve general DP tasks but require hidden dimension scaling as Ω(√L) for general tasks, leading to total complexity Ω(L²), same as standard Transformer.
For arithmetic evaluation, Sparse Transformer can solve with constant hidden dimension, achieving complexity O(L√L).
Linear Transformer for arithmetic evaluation requires hidden dimension Ω(∜L), leading to complexity Ω(L√L).
Under locality assumption (each step depends only on recent m steps), Sparse Transformer can solve with constant hidden dimension, complexity O(mL).
Experiments confirm that efficient Transformers require larger hidden dimensions as problem size increases, especially for non-local tasks like LIS, while standard Transformer does not.
papers.limitation:
The findings for the representative efficient Transformers may not directly transfer to all models with similar designs.
It remains to prove whether the bound for the Linear Transformer under locality can be tightened.
future_direction: Prove tighter bounds for Linear Transformer under locality.
Extend findings to other efficient Transformer designs.
papers.abstract: As transformer-based language models are trained on increasingly large datasets and with vast numbers of parameters, finding more efficient alternatives to the standard Transformer has become very valuable. While many efficient Transformers and Transformer alternatives have been proposed, none provide theoretical guarantees that they are a suitable replacement for the standard Transformer. This makes it challenging to identify when to use a specific model and what directions to prioritize for further investigation. In this paper, we aim to understand the capabilities and limitations of efficient Transformers, specifically the Sparse Transformer and the Linear Transformer. We focus on their reasoning capability as exhibited by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts and follow previous works to model them as Dynamic Programming (DP) problems. Our results show that while these models are expressive enough to solve general DP tasks, contrary to expectations, they require a model size that scales with the problem size. Nonetheless, we identify a class of DP problems for which these models can be more efficient than the standard Transformer. We confirm our theoretical results through experiments on representative DP tasks, adding to the understanding of efficient Transformers' practical strengths and weaknesses.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance.
